#6454. Scientists Discover a Hidden Immune System Difference That Could Explain Why Obesity Affects Men and Women Differently

Scientists have discovered that immune cells in fat tissue behave differently in males and females, potentially helping explain sex-specific responses to obesity.

A type of immune cell best known for its role in allergies and asthma may help explain why obesity affects males and females differently. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside found that certain immune cells in fat tissue appear to protect female mice from obesity-related inflammation, while others become more inflammatory in males fed a high-fat diet.

The findings, published in PNAS Nexus, challenge the long-held assumption that these cells, called eosinophils, perform a relatively narrow range of functions. Instead, their effects may depend on their molecular characteristics, biological sex, and interactions with neighboring immune cells.

Using high-resolution single-cell sequencing, scientists identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue. Each population displayed different patterns of gene activity, suggesting that eosinophils perform specialized functions rather than acting as a single, uniform group.

“Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought,” said Meera Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences at the UCR School of Medicine who co-led the research with biomedical scientist Adam Godzik. “Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find new ways to improve metabolic health.”

In female mice, researchers identified a protective eosinophil population that communicated more effectively with macrophages, another class of immune cells found in fat tissue. This relationship appeared to be supported by RELM alpha, a protein produced by macrophages that may help maintain protective immune activity. Earlier experiments showed that supplying RELM alpha to mice had protective effects, providing additional evidence for its role in regulating the immune environment.

Male mice showed a different response to a high-fat diet. Their fat tissue tended to contain more eosinophil populations associated with inflammation, and these cells displayed gene-expression patterns that suggested weaker protective functions.

“This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present,” said Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair’s laboratory and co-first author of the study. “Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical.”

Although eosinophils have been detected in the fat tissue of people with obesity, scientists have not yet established whether they perform the same protective or inflammatory functions observed in mice. Determining whether similar cell populations exist in humans could help researchers investigate treatments that influence specific immune pathways rather than broadly altering immune activity.

“A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system,” said co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik’s laboratory. “We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients.”

The researchers are now developing three-dimensional adipose organoids, laboratory-grown structures that reproduce certain features of human fat tissue. These models could allow scientists to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and macrophages, and whether modifying those interactions can encourage healthier tissue responses.

“We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses,” said Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

Reference: “Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity” by Rebecca E Ruggiero-Ruff, Xinru Qiu, Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, Djurdjica Coss, Adam Godzik and Meera G Nair, 24 October 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag365

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, UCR School of Medicine, and California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. #6452. Tears of the Lion: Catching the 2026 Leonid Meteors

Why you should watch for the November Leonid meteors this year.

Itâs always worth being vigilant when skywatching in mid- to late November. Every year, a few Leonid meteors punctuate the November sky morning sky around the 17th. These silent harbingers are only a hint at the showerâs true storm potential, which culminates once every three decades.

The Leonid meteor shower can put on a true spectacle, and while 2026 isnât expected to be a âstorm year,â we could be due for some enhanced activity in the late 2020s going into the early 2030s.

The source of the Leonid meteor shower is periodic comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. On a 33 year orbit, comet 55P reaches perihelion 0.975 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun just inside Earthâs orbit once again on May 20, 2031.

Hubble captures Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Credit: NASA/HST/STScI

In 2026 the Moon phase is favorable at 41% illuminated, reaching 1st quarter phase a day after the showerâs peak night on November 16-17th. This means the Moon sets in the west, right as the radiant rises to the east.

The peak of the 2026 Leonids is set for November 17th at 3:00 Universal Time (UT), favoring Europe towards dawn, and North America just a few hours later. While 2026 is projected to be a 20 meteors per hour peak year, you just never know what a particular shower might have in store.

The Leonids are also real fast movers, approaching the Earth nearly head-on with a combined velocity of close to 70 kilometers per second. This is very near the theoretical maximum for inner solar system meteors. Most years only see a paltry 20 or so meteors per hour, though when the parent comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle is near perihelion, great storms are possible.

The Leonids hail from the backwards, question mark-shaped âSickle of Leoâ asterism. The radiant tracks from the +3rd magnitude star Epsilon Leonis past the bright double star Algieba in November. If you can trace a meteorâs flight back to this region, itâs a Leonid.

As an added treat in 2026, the planets Mars and Jupiter are very nearby, along with the bright star Regulus and the antihelion point towards which our planet is currently headed.

The rising Leonid radiant in 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

The Leonids top out with great outbursts every 33 years. A loose definition for a âmeteor stormâ is when the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) tops out at about a 1,000 per hour, which is a fast-paced rate of one meteor every 3-4 seconds. Keep in mind, the ZHR is an extrapolated, ideal rate, assuming dark skies with the showerâs radiant directly overhead at the zenith. Most observers will always see less in reality, as fainter meteors slip by.

Records of the Leonids go all the way back to Arab annuals dating from 902 AD. 1833 saw an historic storm from the shower, as frightened residents along the U.S. Eastern Seaboard awoke to a sky awash in meteors. This single event was not only responsible in part for several religious movements of the day in the U.S., but also helped to push the modern scientific understanding of meteors from a purely atmospheric phenomenon to one originating from space.

A depiction of the Great Leonid Storm of 1833, depicted in 1889 by Adolf Vollmy. Credit: Public Domain.

The morning of November 17, 1966 saw a formidable performance from the shower, with observed rates over the southwestern U.S. topping out at an estimated 160,000 per hour (!)

I still remember catching the 1998 Leonids from the deserts of Kuwait, a year before the advertised outburst in 1999. The meteors lit up the desert floor just seconds apart towards sunrise with brilliant photo-flash flares. The spectacle continued right up until dawn. To date, it was still one of the best meteor showers Iâve ever witnessed.

Are we in for another great âmeteor stormâ in or around 2033? Well, we passed the mid-point in 2017. We did see a steady uptick in meteor activity through the late 1990s leading up to 1999. A caveat, however is in order with the approach of the Leonids in the early 2030s. Current models suggest we wonât see any great storms on the 2031 and 2064 passes of the comet, with 2099 being the next great âstorm yearâ. We may, however, still see respectable showers in excess of 100 per hour in the early 2030s laid down by older streams, topping the annual Perseid and Geminid meteors.

A Leonid double-shot. Credit: Eliot Herman

Observing a meteor shower is as simple as laying back and watching the sky, no special equipment needed. All you need is clear, dark skies and patience. Youâll see more in the early morning hours, as Earth hurdles headlong into the oncoming meteor stream. Imaging Leonids is a simple as setting up a tripod-mounted DSLR camera equipped with a wide-field lens to take long exposure shots of the sky, and seeing what turns up. An intervalometer hand control works great to automate this process.

An all-sky capture featuring a Leonid meteor. Credit: Eliot Herman.

Finally, be sure to count and record what you see, and send those observations to the International Meteor Organization.

Weâll see what the coming years has in store for the November Leonid meteors. One thing is for certain: youâll see zero meteors if you donât try. Time will tell if the coming years see the Leonids roar once again.

David Dickinson is a freelance science writer and long-time sky watcher. He has built telescopes and observatories, chased eclipses, and travels and observes with his wife, Myscha, on a mission to get âeyes on the skyâ worldwide. #6451. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6450. Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds

Robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.

Tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.

This isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.

Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.

But this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.

TeCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.

But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.

Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.

This unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.

But when they combine together, they unlock whole new operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.

Those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.

Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel

That being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. Currently, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do plan to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.

#6449. Your Brain Chemistry Could Change How You Understand Language

A single word can overturn your understanding of a sentence, and your brain chemistry may shape how hard you work to make sense of it again.

Even a single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, forcing the brain to rethink what it just read. But how efficiently the brain handles these grammatical surprises may depend partly on its chemistry.

A study published in PNAS found that increasing dopamine and noradrenaline (catecholamines) strengthened a brain response associated with untangling ambiguous grammar. Researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (MPI-PL) in Nijmegen observed the largest effects in healthy adults with lower baseline working memory capacity.

“Catecholamines are known to regulate attention, working memory, and cognitive control, but their role in language remains poorly understood,” says Peter Hagoort, senior investigator and director emeritus of MPI-PL’s Neurobiology of Language Department and the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behavior.

“Our earlier work suggested that catecholamines can affect semantic aspects of sentence comprehension. Whether these neuromodulatory systems also influence syntactic processing—how the brain combines words into grammatical structures—was largely unknown.”

Understanding a sentence involves more than knowing what its words mean. Readers also have to work out how those words fit together, sometimes revising an interpretation as new information arrives. The researchers used temporarily ambiguous “garden-path” sentences to examine that process.

Consider “The fan attacked the drummer, and the guitarist packed the instruments up.” When the words appear one at a time, readers may initially group “the drummer and the guitarist” together as the people being attacked. The word “packed” reveals that the guitarist is instead performing a separate action, requiring readers to rebuild their interpretation.

To test whether brain chemistry influences this revision, the team recruited 30 healthy adults. Each completed two sessions, once after taking methylphenidate, a stimulant commonly prescribed for ADHD that increases catecholamine levels, and once after taking a placebo.

Participants read ambiguous and unambiguous sentences and answered comprehension questions after each one. Meanwhile, researchers recorded their brain activity using EEG (electroencephalography), allowing them to examine the response at the precise word that exposed the grammatical ambiguity.

After methylphenidate, participants showed a stronger P600 response at the critical word, such as “packed.” This well-known EEG signal is associated with demanding grammatical processing and reflects increased cognitive effort. Its enhancement suggests that higher catecholamine levels changed how the brain recruited resources to resolve the sentence.

The increase was greatest among participants whose working memory capacity was lower before treatment.

“The findings suggest that catecholaminergic systems contribute to the dynamic allocation of cognitive resources during syntactic processing,” says Hagoort. “Their influence on language therefore appears to extend beyond semantic processing to syntactic unification, and the magnitude of this effect may depend on individual baseline working memory performance.”

“The results support the development of neuropharmacolinguistics as a field linking neuromodulatory systems to language processing.”

Reference: “Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing” by Yingying Tan, Ashley G. Lewis, Iris C. Schmits, Robert-Jan Verkes, Roshan Cools and Peter Hagoort, 22 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2606806123

#6448. A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

A geographer calls it Aquaterra. For 120,000 years, early humans lived there—then the oceans swallowed it.

Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke. Trying to leave no stone unturned, I explored the former colony’s dedicated National Historic Site, poured over archives of antique maps, and even took in a lavish outdoor stage production.

Ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks. Yet one moment from that trip has never been far from my mind, and it reshaped how I thought about our quest for answers about early human history.

It came about during a conversation with Dr. Eric Klingelhofer, a respected scholar and Vice President for Research with The First Colony Foundation. Dr. Klingelhofer had overseen several excavations that yielded remnants of Roanoke, but he was worried that many once-buried artifacts had already been claimed by a much more powerful force.

“Before my retirement,” he told me, “I attended a UNESCO-backed conference on Bonaire in the Dutch West Indies. These causes, rising sea levels and storm surges, plus coastal overdevelopment, endangered every island, as most prehistoric and early colonial sites lie close to the sea.” As we sat there on tranquil, federally protected land, it was hard for me to feel the urgency at the time, but he stressed that we were in a race against time. “At Fort Raleigh,”—the name the National Parks Service gave the National Historic Site—“coastal erosion has already swallowed up excavation units we had dug in 2007. The rate of loss is about twenty feet in twenty years—and it may be increasing.”

After our conversation, I walked along the island’s shoreline, struck by the thought that although I might be walking the same land as those colonists, the landscape wasn’t really the same. Their shoreline likely sat yards farther out than the one I strolled, and as the water swept that land away, it took with it our chance to learn more about the people who once stood there.

In the study of history, we too often focus on the preservation or replication of what was once on a certain parcel of land, taking it as a given that the land itself stayed constant. We spend all our time debating whether the proverbial Ship of Theseus is still the same after centuries of repairs, never stopping to question if the shoreline of Delos on which he landed still remains.

Yet, recent studies have emerged to remind us that even in the absence of human intervention, the world looked different to the peoples of the past than it does to us today.

The scale of this dilemma, the problem of our submerged history, is far greater than a single island in North Carolina, or a single colony from the 1500s. Our whole understanding of early humankind may be built on faulty ground, due specifically to how much of that ground is now underwater. But don’t let your thoughts drift to that Platonic idea of Atlantis; the proper term, as The Atlantic recently reminded us, is Aquaterra.

In 2014, the geographer Jerome E. Dobson mounted a case for the recognition of a global landmass he dubbed Aquaterra, a term he first proposed in 1999. In “Aquaterra Incognita,” Dobson argued that “all landmasses are defined by time as well as space,” and therefore, since “so little is known about the seacoast where a significant portion of humankind surely dwelled for the better part of 120,000 years,” we should properly recognize and name the 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass that once hosted the earliest human civilizations.

When we think about the ice ages that have cycled across Earth’s history, we can easily picture the glaciers and ice sheets that formed, but we rarely consider where all that water came from. During an ice age, sea levels drop, exposing land that’s now underwater. As a result, the shorelines early humans knew looked very different from the ones we see today.

The lowlands these glaciers exposed were not bereft of life, either. The ecosystems they once supported varied, from grasslands to wetlands, forests to estuaries. They attracted wildlife, and later, early human civilizations. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” Dobson writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.”

When the glaciers melted and sea levels rose again, naturally, early humans abandoned their soon-to-be-submerged settlements. But that doesn’t mean we should simply ignore what once stood there. “It would not change the timeline of human progress if, for instance, cities were found as low as -50 meters, since Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were that low,” Dobson notes. What could revise that timeline, he notes, is “the possibility that precursors of major innovations may exist at even lower depths.”

“One intriguing possibility is pottery,” he proposes:

All this talk about “possibility,” of course, makes the benefits of recognizing Aquaterra seem entirely theoretical. Yet in just the last few years, the archeological world received a stirring reminder that the land we can see is not the only land there ever was, and that whole chapters of our history may have been claimed by the sea.

In 2021, Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith published “The magnificent seven: Marine submerged precontact sites found by systematic geoarchaeology in the Americas.” The study documented not one or two but seven projects, in North America alone, that had found traces of precontact life now drowned beneath the continental shelf. Each of the seven projects worked “from the terrestrially known, to the submerged unknown.” Using methodical but varied mapping and modeling techniques, researchers predicted where people might once have lived, then searched for proof with underwater surveys, sediment cores, and even hands-on excavations.

One of the research efforts happened in the Gulf of Mexico’s paleo-Sabine River. Over the course of a decade, from 1976 to 1986, it turned up “charred wood and vegetation, nut hulls, seeds, fish scales, and bone from fish, reptiles, birds, and small mammals,” some of which dated back 9,000 years. Soon after, researchers in Belize found the drowned outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings, which turned out to be Classic-period Maya salt works now sitting underwater. Other research discussed in the study uncovered stone tools, campsites, and even a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.

To truly understand human history, we can’t keep digging only in the land we can see. We also have to search for the land our ancestors knew, much of which now lies beneath the waves. That calls for a change in mindset and a rethinking of how archaeology works. As seas keep rising, how many more once-inhabited places will slip beneath the surface, taking with them secrets as recent as Roanoke’s? If we don’t change course now, the sites we have yet to excavate may be written off by tomorrow’s scholars as mere seafloor.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts. Nature, 659. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5

#6446. Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.

One of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.

Despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.

The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.

Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.

Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.

New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.

This image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille)

When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.

That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.

"We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.

This is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.

The researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.

"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions."

The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.

The researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.

Astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.

"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.

This is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.

"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.

More observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide important observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.

"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

#6445. Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.

California is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada. But scientists are discovering that the state’s insect diversity is far greater than previously believed.

A new study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates. Scientists have formally described only about two-thirds of them. Led by researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, the study also found that nearly every location sampled had its own distinct insect community.

The findings suggest that conserving California’s insect life will require protecting a wide range of habitats. Even places with similar climates and landscapes can harbor different species, making it difficult for any single protected area to represent the state’s extraordinary diversity.

The research is the first publication from the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project with an ambitious goal: collect and identify every insect species in California. Although insects are the most diverse group of animals on land, they remain underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments.

Researchers used DNA barcoding on more than one million insect specimens. The technique compares short sections of DNA to help distinguish species, giving scientists a way to investigate diversity that can be difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

The effort brought together the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, and California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Researchers gathered tissue samples from museum collections, deployed Malaise traps across 72 ecoregions, and made collecting expeditions to 454 additional locations statewide.

Museum specimens extended the project’s reach beyond what researchers could collect in the field. Fresh sampling added another essential piece, with volunteers helping keep traps operating week after week. Although Malaise traps capture insects passively, collecting their contents and maintaining them takes sustained effort.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” says study co-author Giar-Ann Kung, the museum’s entomology collections manager.

Kung joined researchers and volunteers across California in setting traps and collecting insects. Some participants maintained sampling sites for years, providing a continuity that the research team could not have achieved alone.

“There are people like Sara Fairchild and Michael Nance who managed a Malaise trap for over three years at a site in the high desert, which is the longest continuous site for the project. That could not have been accomplished without them.”

To explore how insect diversity varies across California, the researchers compared ecoregions, areas grouped by the Environmental Protection Agency according to shared ecosystem characteristics. They used Level 3 classifications, including the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. Of these regions, the Mojave Basin and Range had the greatest number of insect species.

Although similar environments shared some patterns, each region had its own mix of insects. “The deserts are kind of more similar to each other, and the mountains in northern California are a little bit more similar to each other, but every part of the state hosts a really different insect fauna,” says Dr. Barkdull.

Those differences also appeared at a smaller scale, with individual collecting sites within the same ecoregion harboring distinct insect communities. Together, the findings highlight the need to protect a wide range of California’s wild places.

Reference: “DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California’s insect biodiversity remains undiscovered” by Austin J. #6444. LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date

An international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.

For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.

This new view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.

The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON

"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.

In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This new view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.

The other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.

The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON

According to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.

The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

#6442. Scientists Develop a Groundbreaking Rechargeable Battery That Runs on Vitamin B12

The same vitamin found in everyday foods could eventually help store surplus renewable electricity, after an experimental zinc-air battery using B12 completed up to 250 recharge cycles.

The search for safer, more sustainable batteries is leading scientists to some unexpected places, including the chemistry of vitamins. Researchers at the University of Córdoba in Spain have found that vitamin B12, a nutrient essential to human health, can also help power a rechargeable battery. Their experimental design completed up to 250 charge and discharge cycles, opening another possibility for future energy storage technology.

The researchers developed a zinc-air battery, which generates electricity through chemical reactions involving zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. Unlike conventional batteries that store all their reactive materials internally, zinc-air batteries draw oxygen from the environment. This makes them lighter and gives them high energy density, meaning they can store substantial energy relative to their weight. They are already used in small devices such as hearing aids.

Zinc also offers advantages because it is abundant and recyclable. These batteries use nonflammable, water-based electrolytes, making them potentially safer than conventional lithium-ion batteries, whose raw material extraction raises economic, social, and environmental concerns.

Making zinc-air batteries rechargeable, however, presents a challenge. They need a catalyst, a substance that helps chemical reactions proceed, that can support both the production of electricity and the reverse process needed to recharge the battery.

Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, offered a possible solution because its molecular structure contains cobalt (III), a form of the metal cobalt that helps drive these reactions. Although better known for its role in nutrition, B12 is produced naturally by certain bacteria and manufactured commercially for food and pharmaceutical applications. Found in foods of animal origin, it is used to address nutritional deficiencies and has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because it can help reduce fatigue.

Researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero explained that vitamin B12 “has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen”.

The difficulty was keeping the vitamin inside the battery. Because B12 dissolves readily in water, it could not simply be added to a battery that uses a water-based electrolyte. The researchers solved this problem by attaching the vitamin to single-walled carbon nanotubes, extremely thin carbon structures that hold it in place while allowing it to support the chemical reactions. Their approach mimicked “the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins.”

The prototype was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba’s Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). As study author Manuel Cano Luna explained, “we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries.”

This is the group’s third battery prototype using a biological molecule as a catalyst. Earlier experiments involved hemoglobin, which contains iron (II), and catalase, which contains iron (III). The key advance with vitamin B12 is that the resulting battery can be recharged, completing up to 250 cycles in the researchers’ tests.

Although the prototype remains experimental, the findings suggest that naturally occurring molecules could contribute to cheaper, more sustainable energy storage systems. With further development, rechargeable zinc-air batteries could eventually help store surplus electricity from renewable energy sources, addressing one of the challenges of transitioning toward cleaner energy.

Reference: “A vitamin B12-based air electrode for high-performance rechargeable zinc–air batteries” by García-Caballero, Valentín, López-León, Miguel, G. Argudo, Pablo, Camacho, Luis, Rodríguez Mellado, José M., Martín-Romero, Maria T., Abad, José, Fernández Romero, Antonio J. and Cano, Manuel, , Journal of Materials Chemistry A. DOI: 10.1039/d6ta02773c

#6441. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6439. A Tiny Region Deep Inside Your Brain Helps Decide What You Remember

Scientists have discovered that a small brain region best known for processing emotions plays a surprisingly broad role in determining which experiences become lasting memories.

The brain records countless sights and experiences every day, yet only a fraction become lasting memories. Scientists have now identified a pattern of neural activity that helps predict what will be remembered, pointing to a much broader role for a brain region traditionally associated with emotions and fear.

The discovery, made by researchers at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University and published in Nature Neuroscience, centers on the amygdala, a walnut-sized structure deep within the temporal lobe. The findings suggest that specialized neurons in this region help determine which new experiences are selected for long-term memory storage.

The amygdala has long been known for its involvement in emotional and social behavior, particularly the processing of fear. Its contribution to memory was generally thought to center on emotionally significant experiences. The new research indicates that its influence extends to more ordinary visual experiences, even those without an obvious emotional component.

Researchers identified neurons that respond preferentially to certain types of images, including faces, animals, and landscapes. When these neurons reacted more strongly to an image from their preferred category, participants were more likely to remember that image later. This suggests that the strength of these specialized neural responses helps predict which experiences will remain accessible in memory.

“Our results demonstrate that the activity of specific kinds of neurons in the amygdala predicts, while the person sees an image for the first time, whether that image will later be remembered,” said Ueli Rutishauser, PhD,>

To investigate how the brain selects information for storage, scientists analyzed recordings from 112 patients who had electrodes implanted in their brains to monitor epileptic seizures. These electrodes allowed researchers to measure the electrical activity of individual neurons while participants viewed unfamiliar images.

Later that same day, participants were asked to recall the pictures they had seen. By comparing their memory performance with the earlier neural recordings, investigators could identify patterns of amygdala activity associated with successful recall. The findings were replicated in two separate datasets, strengthening the evidence for the relationship between these neurons and memory formation.

The unusually large collection of single-neuron recordings was assembled through a multi-institutional research consortium led by Cedars-Sinai and supported by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies (BRAIN) initiative. Jiayang Xiao, PhD, led the research as the study’s first author.

“This is an impactful study that provides mechanistic insight into the role of the human amygdala—a region commonly associated with emotional responses—in determining which experiences and stimuli become lasting episodic memories. This rigorous human neuroscience study, which uses next-generation tools, has high potential to move discovery toward measurable health impacts,” said Mauricio Rangel-Gomez, PhD, program officer at NIH.

The results raise the possibility that disruptions to amygdala activity contribute to memory difficulties associated with neurological conditions. Although the recordings establish a relationship between neuronal responses and later recall, further research is needed to determine whether modifying these responses could improve memory.

“Our findings have important clinical implications, as the memory impairments seen in disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and temporal lobe epilepsy might be partly due to disrupted processes within the amygdala,” said Rutishauser, also a professor of Neurosurgery. “The amygdala might therefore be a suitable new target for treating these disorders using neuromodulation and/or cellular therapies.”

An additional question is whether the same memory selection process operates across different senses. The current experiments focused on visual information, and Rutishauser said future studies could examine whether the amygdala also helps determine which sounds and smells become lasting memories.

“This study’s insights are the latest in a long line of research led by Cedars-Sinai and collaborators dedicated to revealing how human memory functions,” said Adam Mamelak, MD,> Reference: “Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success” by Jiayang Xiao, Jonathan Daume, Yousef Salimpour, Natalia Kurilenko, Clayton Mosher, William S. Anderson, Taufik A. Valiante, Adam N. Mamelak and Ueli Rutishauser, 27 October 2026, Nature Neuroscience. DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02493-9
