Mitochondria can become compromised in a number of medical conditions. What if they could be replaced like batteries?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newborn baby's heart is roughly the size of a walnut — which makes open-heart surgery challenging.

Each year, about 10,000 babies in the United States are born with critical heart defects that may require surgery to fix, often fairly soon after birth. In these infants, the two major arteries of the heart could have swapped positions or the left side of the heart may be far too small to pump properly.

Even if their surgeries go well, these babies face perilous recoveries. A complication can arise when blood flows back into the repaired heart, triggering what's known as an ischemia-reperfusion injury. This can stun the organ, triggering extensive damage that requires doctors to place the baby on a life-support machine that pumps and infuses oxygen into blood to sub in for the hampered heart and lungs. Only about 40% of newborns make it off the machine, because often, their tiny hearts don't recover.

Doctors and scientists at Boston Children's Hospital have been working to improve those odds using a creative idea: replacing the fuel source in damaged heart cells to help them bounce back from injury. That fuel source is mitochondria, the "batteries" found in most cells in the body. In this case, the mitochondria are isolated from an abdominal muscle and then injected directly into the heart.

As of April, 17 babies have undergone this procedure, and 80% made it off ECMO. It's too soon to say if the treatment improves overall survival rates, but the early data hints that it might. A clinical trial is currently underway.

James McCully (left) and his colleague Dr. Sitaram Emani of Boston Children's Hospital have developed a technique to transplant mitochondria into the hearts of children recovering from surgery.

"The first one or two for me were pretty nerve-wracking," said James McCully, a research associate at Boston Children's Hospital and associate professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School whose pioneering work paved the way for these procedures. His team isolates and purifies the mitochondria that a surgical team then transplants into patients.

"But you know, the heart comes back — you can actually almost see it coming back" in real time, he told Live Science. A heart deprived of energy looks pallid, while a freshly rejuvenated heart blushes a healthy pink.

Baby heart infusions are just one example of the promise of "mitochondrial transplantation." Following McCully's lead, other scientists have started investigating whether infusions of mitochondria could revitalize donated organs destined for transplantation, help stroke patients recover, and treat kids with devastating diseases. This work is still highly experimental, and its route to regulatory approval remains unclear.

But at its core is a straightforward idea: When a battery dies, you replace it.

The human body contains tens of trillions of cells, most of which contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. Following some back-of-the-envelope math, that means the total potential energy in each person "is the equivalent of a lightning bolt," Douglas Wallace, director of the Center for Mitochondrial and Epigenomic Medicine at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told attendees last year at a symposium on mitochondrial medicine.

Mitochondria, in a word, are powerful. They produce most of the chemical energy used by complex cells by churning out a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The idea of transferring these fuel factories from one cell to another as a medical treatment emerged less than two decades ago — but cells have been doing such swaps on their own for eons.

A leading theory posits that mitochondria evolved from simple microbes. And today, they still retain distinctly microbial features.

Dr. Jon Brestoff, an associate professor of pathology and immunology and director of the Immunometabolism Initiative at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, describes this ability to move from cell to cell as a relic of mitochondria's bacterial past. "It is hypothesized that mitochondria transfer has likely been retained throughout evolution of eukaryotic life," the huge domain of life that includes all plants, fungi, protists and animals, Brestoff told Live Science.

Mitochondria are the powerhouses of nearly all complex cells on Earth, and there are a few theories as to how they adopted that ubiquitous role. A leading idea posits that, some 1.5 billion to 2 billion years ago, one simple cell engulfed another. The bacterial cell that got swallowed carried a circular loop of DNA inside its membrane, and that captured cell later became what we now know as the mitochondrion. The new organelle enabled cells to take advantage of the abundance of oxygen on our planet by converting it into usable fuel.

Mitochondria retained bacteria-like features, such as having their own DNA and membranes. But in 2006, researchers reported that mitochondria can also exit their "host" and survive the journey into a totally different cell — a phenomenon known as mitochondrial transfer.

"That was a complete revolution in thinking," said Dr. Lance Becker, professor and Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "With that notion that mitochondria might be mobile, that they might cross boundaries, that they might go from one cell to another cell, came the possibility that maybe that was something we could use to help people."

The 2006 study showed that cells that had been depleted of their own mitochondrial DNA could obtain healthy mitochondria from neighboring cells. After receiving other cells' powerhouses, the once-depleted cells were able to conduct energetically costly processes, such as cell division.

This research provided the first evidence that one cell can "donate" metabolic properties to its neighbor by sending over a fresh batch of mitochondria. Scientists once thought cells had to make all of their own mitochondria, but now, "I think cells have the ability to 'put their hand up' when they need mitochondria," Becker told Live Science.

Jon Brestoff is studying the use of mitochondrial transplantation for genetic diseases that impair the function of these cellular powerhouses.

Because those first experiments were done in lab dishes, initially, "it was unclear whether or not it was really biologically meaningful or relevant," Brestoff said. But within the past five to six years, improved tools and techniques have enabled scientists to watch mitochondrial transfer unfold within living organisms, he noted. It's been shown that cells of the same type can exchange mitochondria, as can cells of different types.

As scientists' fundamental understanding of mitochondrial transfer grew, the notion of doing the same thing therapeutically gained more traction.

"That procedure," Brestoff said, "is rooted in the biology of mitochondria transfer."

Just two years after the landmark 2006 paper, McCully's research group released data that hinted at the medicinal potential of mitochondrial transplantation.

Since then, these complementary lines of research — the foundational biology and the preclinical investigation — have continued in parallel. McCully's preclinical work helped to inspire other labs to explore the use of mitochondrial transplantation for a range of medical applications, including organ transplants and treatments for stroke and genetic disease.

McCully is "the pioneer — the guru of the field," said Dr. Giuseppe Orlando, a professor of surgery and regenerative medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who is exploring mitochondrial transplantation as a way to maintain the integrity of transplant organs.

McCully's road to mitochondrial transplantation started in the 1980s. As a molecular biologist, he wanted to uncover mechanisms that protect the heart from damage, particularly when the organ's oxygen supply is compromised — such as during ischemia, or low blood flow. With an eye on older adults, he wanted to spare patients' heart tissue from the damage and cell death that can occur before and during heart surgery.

It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going.

McCully and his collaborators initially "didn't care about the mitochondria one iota," he said. They were more focused on the nucleus, the control center that houses most of a cell's DNA, and its influence on cellular pathways that might boost the heart's resilience to ischemia. But "what we found was that everything we did started coming back to the mitochondria," he said.

They found that ischemia triggers damage and dysfunction in mitochondria that persists even after the heart's oxygen supply is restored; this dysfunction ultimately kills cells. The damaged mitochondria swell up, leak their innards, and set off a chain reaction that causes a cell to self-destruct.

McCully and colleagues observed that biological pathways that seemed to reduce this cell death often centered on the mitochondria. "We were looking around at either pathways upstream of the mitochondria or downstream of the mitochondria," he said.

So, logically, they started looking directly at mitochondria, studying what the organelle looks like before, during and after ischemia. One day, while isolating mitochondria from a laboratory pig, the animal developed fibrillation, meaning its heart began beating very quickly, with an uncoordinated and rapid rhythm. The team tried to reset the heart's rhythm with electric shocks and medications, to no avail. But McCully had an idea.

"At that point in time, the heart's kind of [got a] gray pallor, and it looks dead," he said. "And I said, 'Go upstairs; grab some of those mitochondria that we've isolated from the non-ischemic type. Just bring them down.'" They'd previously gathered some healthy mitochondria from the same pig, in hopes of generating a "before-and-after" picture of ischemia. Instead, McCully suspended those healthy mitochondria in a solution and then injected them directly into the pig's fibrillating heart.

"And the heart came back — started beating normally. It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going," he said.

Surgeons sample a small piece of muscle from the patient. That muscle will serve as the source of healthy mitochondria.

After mitochondria have been isolated from the muscle sample, they are prepared in a syringe and injected into the heart tissue.

That serendipitous experiment led to a formal test of the technique in rabbit hearts, the results of which were published in 2008. In the study, they introduced healthy mitochondria to the rabbits' hearts during ischemia, just before reperfusion — when blood is reintroduced into the oxygen-starved tissue. They found that the mitochondria improved the organs' recovery and reduced tissue death. Further research in animals suggested that mitochondria that originated from one type of tissue, like liver tissue or skeletal muscle, could be introduced to other tissue types, such as cardiac muscle.

After seeing McCully's results in various animal experiments, including more with pigs, Dr. Pedro del Nido, chair of cardiac surgery at Boston Children's and a professor of child surgery at Harvard Medical School, approached him about testing the technique in human patients — namely, in babies on a life-support machine known as ECMO.

"He saw it in the animals; he saw what was going on," McCully said. "And he deemed it as being a possible intervention to save these kids."

They sought permission from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to test the procedure and cleared the required regulatory hurdles. The process was made slightly easier because the mitochondria were coming from the patients' own bodies, not from a donor, McCully noted. Once given the go-ahead, they set forth with the help of Dr. Sitaram Emani, a heart surgeon at Boston Children's. The first procedure took place in 2014.

During each procedure, Emani and the surgical team collect a small sample of skeletal muscle from the patient, and McCully then isolates whole mitochondria from the tissue and prepares them in a syringe. He refined the isolation technique so the time from collecting the muscle sample to injecting mitochondria is only 30 minutes. Lately, the team has been developing a technique they can perform in the operating room, rather than in a lab, which could cut the time to 20 minutes. Emani uses various tests, including echocardiography, to see which areas of the heart tissue move the least, and injects mitochondria straight into those areas.

"It's great to be able to see something you've done and worked on for so many years actually provide a benefit," McCully said.

Dr. Giuseppe Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplantation could serve as a potential method for fortifying donated organs that are intended for transplant patients.

While McCully is trying to protect infant hearts, other scientists want to do the same for other organs — including those destined for transplant surgeries.

To Orlando, mitochondria represent a potential way to make donated kidneys work better. "In transplant medicine, one of the major issues is making sure that the organs that are procured are well stored and kept viable until implantation," said Orlando, who is also president of the Cell Transplant and Regenerative Medicine Society.

Maintaining an organ's viability means preserving mitochondrial function as much as possible, but the transplantation process is tough on the organelles. "That energy plant is damaged. So it's pretty obvious that you should start thinking about a way to replace the damaged mitochondria," Orlando said.

Donated organs suffer some damage when they're unplugged from the donors' bloodstream, in part because this cuts off mitochondria's crucial oxygen supply. And then, paradoxically, the donor organs also get damaged when they're plugged into the recipient's bloodstream. That's because the fast flow of blood triggers the production of free radicals — unstable molecules that damage tissues.

While healthy organs normally produce some free radicals, reperfusion unleashes a flood. "It's more than the organ can bear and sustain," Orlando explained. This damage contributes to a phenomenon called delayed graft function, in which a transplanted kidney doesn't work right away so the patient ends up needing dialysis in the first week after surgery.

"You want to make sure that the kidney wakes up faster," Orlando said. That's where mitochondria come in.

Orlando was introduced to the idea of mitochondrial transplantation around 2019 through a collaboration with Dr. Benedetta Bussolati, a nephrologist and full professor of laboratory medicine at the University of Turin in Italy. Her lab had been studying mitochondrial transplantation in isolated kidney cells in lab experiments, and they reached out to Orlando about extending that work to lab animals.

In pigs, the researchers ran experiments in which the animals' kidneys were collected and stored in the same way human kidneys commonly would be prior to being transplanted. One set of kidneys received a placebo treatment, while another got an infusion of mitochondria from the donor pigs' muscle tissue. Upon being reperfused, the treated kidneys produced fewer free radicals and accrued less damage than the untreated kidneys did, the team reported in 2023.

They backed up this finding by analyzing RNA, a molecule that reflects which genes are active in cells. Compared with the untreated kidneys, the treated kidneys showed greater activity in genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and lower activity in genes involved in repairing injuries.

Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplanations could help organs "wake up" faster after being transferred from an organ donor to a recipient.

Some groups are exploring mitochondrial transplantation in other donor organs, like the lungs — specifically, lungs treated with "ex vivo perfusion" (EVP), an emerging approach that helps retain the viability of transplant organs. Rather than placing a donor organ in a cooler of ice, as is generally standard, EVP flushes an organ with nutrient- and oxygen-rich fluid, helping to maintain its function until the transplant surgery. In lab experiments with pig and human lungs, scientists found that introducing fresh mitochondria during EVP further improved the organs' function while reducing inflammation and free radicals.

Across different organ transplants, Orlando sees mitochondria as a potential means to improve patient outcomes and expand the pool of available organs. There are scenarios in which would-be organ donors die unexpectedly of cardiac arrest and their organs are damaged in the process; mitochondrial transplants may help make such organs fit for patients, Orlando has said.

In the near term, Orlando and his colleagues are continuing to study the basic science of mitochondrial transplantation for this clinical purpose; they've also been cleared to run a clinical trial with donor kidneys but need more funds to proceed.

Looking to the more distant future, he and other experts in the field envision a world where transplant organs can be bioengineered and stored in banks, ready and waiting for the patients who need them, Orlando said. If that vision materializes, he suggested, mitochondrial transplants might be useful for preparing banked organs for transplantation "by giving them kind of an energy boost."

If infusions of fresh mitochondria could help the heart, kidney and lungs, what about the brain? That's the question Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues at the University of Washington School of Medicine (UW Medicine) want to answer.

Walker, a clinical professor of neurological surgery, treats patients who have had ischemic strokes, which are caused by blood clots blocking blood flow to the brain. The immediate aim of post-stroke treatment is to clear out the blocked "pipe" and restore circulation to the brain as quickly as possible, she said. But no matter how quickly this is done, some brain cells are damaged. And once the blood clot is removed, the brain may then suffer a reperfusion injury.

Standard treatments can dissolve the clot but don't protect the brain, Walker said. "What about all those cells that are maybe not quite dead — they're on the verge of maybe dying? What can we do to support those guys?" she asked.

The UW Medicine team had heard about McCully's work in Boston and wondered if something similar could be applied in stroke patients. But while heart surgery exposes the tissue in need of new mitochondria, accessing the brain is trickier. "You don't do a craniotomy to give an IV medicine," Walker told Live Science.

But Walker realized that a harmful downstream effect of stroke might provide an opportunity for treatment. Immediately after a stroke, the brain's protective shield — known as the blood-brain barrier — becomes more permeable than usual, allowing more substances to pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue. That might open a door for mitochondrial transplantation.

One method of treating ischemic strokes is to physically remove the clot using a procedure called a thrombectomy, which a surgeon is preparing for in the photo above. Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues tried combining this approach with mitochondrial transplantation.

A 2023 mouse study spearheaded by University of Virginia researchers and co-authored by Walker backed this idea, finding that mitochondria entered the brain after stroke and integrated into brain cells. These mitochondria had been gathered from muscle tissue, as in McCully's studies, and introduced to the brain via an artery. The treatment increased ATP production while reducing cell death caused by the stroke, compared with untreated mice's brains.

This work paved the way to the first trial using mitochondrial transplant in the human brain. The small safety trial included adult patients who'd had ischemic strokes and underwent thrombectomies ‪—‬ surgeries to remove the clots from their blood vessels. Four received mitochondrial transplants during their procedures and 12 did not. Mitochondria were injected near the site of each patient's stroke, into the closest branch of one of the brain's major arteries.

No negative side effects were tied to the transplants, hinting that the procedure is safe in humans. "But the next question is, how do we understand if it helps? And those are harder trials to design," Walker said. That's partly because the transplants are tacked onto the clot-removal procedure, so it's difficult to separate their effects from those of the clot removal itself, she noted.

Future trials will also need to explore exactly where the transplanted mitochondria end up in the human brain, how well they function once inside brain cells, and how the dose and timing of the transplant affect patients' outcomes, the trial runners wrote in their report. For the moment, Walker said her team is focused on exploring the safety aspects of the approach and have no further trials planned at this time.

Beyond heart defects, transplant organs and stroke, researchers are looking to mitochondrial transplantation as a solution for genetic conditions that harm mitochondria directly. Brestoff and colleagues are investigating the therapy's potential for treating Leigh syndrome, a rare neurological condition caused by genetic mutations that disrupt the fuel-producing machinery in mitochondria.

"Those kids have a terrible prognosis," Brestoff said. Most children with the most common form of the syndrome, whose symptoms show up by age 2, die by age 3. There is no cure for the syndrome, and treatments to relieve its symptoms are limited. So if it works, mitochondrial transplantation could fill a big gap.

So far, the approach shows promise in lab mice with a severe form of Leigh syndrome, improving the rodents' function and extending their median lifespan by 19% to 24%, the researchers demonstrated in 2024. They're now studying the approach in cells derived from patients with the disease.

I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter.

Some companies, such as Israel-headquartered Minovia Therapeutics, are already running clinical trials with patients with other types of mitochondrial disease. Minovia is running one with children with Pearson syndrome, in which missing mitochondrial DNA hinders the function of bone marrow, which normally makes blood and immune cells.

While patients with a heart or brain problem may be able to pluck mitochondria from healthy muscles, people with mitochondrial disease don't necessarily have healthy mitochondria to spare. Especially for these patients, getting mitochondria from other people ‪—‬ known as heterologous transplantation ‪—‬ likely makes the most sense. What's more, for transplantation to be used widely for any purpose, there would need to be an "off-the-shelf" mitochondrial product available, Brestoff said.

Such a product could eliminate the step in Boston Children's heart procedure where mitochondria have to be isolated from a patient while they're waiting, open on an operating table. "Getting them from the recipient can sometimes be problematic, because the recipients are sick. All the organs, all the tissue is quite distressed," McCully noted. A standardized and safety-tested mitochondrial product would therefore be a boon for the field.

Brestoff is on the scientific advisory board of LUCA Science, a company developing mitochondria as therapeutic agents, and a consultant for Cellergy Therapeutics, which is making mitochondrial products to combat conditions from muscle degeneration and aging. These companies exemplify the effort to come up with ready-made products that could someday bring the therapy to more patients.

A shift to heterologous transplantation does raise concerns about immune reactions. "You have some variations in the proteins that are present in your mitochondria that I don't have," Brestoff noted. "So it is possible that our immune systems recognize heterologous mitochondria as non-self."

But McCully doesn't expect immune reactions to be a big problem, based on his research in animals. "I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter," he said. Early trial results from Minovia and others suggest heterologous transplantations come with minimal side effects, at least at doses tested so far.

Another roadblock is that the FDA has not approved any organelles as therapies yet, so the standards and regulatory framework for the field are still being established, Brestoff said.

Despite that hurdle, the field has advanced significantly since its start as a niche, theoretical interest and then a highly experimental procedure for the sickest newborns. Scientists are now exploring the treatment as a solution to many common conditions, from rheumatoid arthritis to chronic pain.

Becker compared the state of the field to the early days of organ transplantation.

"It just turned out that it was revolutionary, when all of a sudden you could just give a person a kidney transplant," he said. "I think it's going to be kind of similar with mitochondria."

#6394. No Central Air? No Sweat. These Tested Window Air Conditioners Cool Down Spaces Fast

We got our hands on multiple units and looked for models that are quiet, energy-efficient, and easy to install.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it’s really hot or humid out, opening a window or turning on a fan only gets you so far, especially when your house feels like it’s holding onto heat long after the sun goes down. If you’ve ever tried to sleep in a hot, airless room, you know how quickly feeling “a little warm” turns into being completely miserable. For homeowners and renters without central air conditioning, the standard solutions are typically ductless air conditioners, freestanding units, or window air conditioners.

Window air conditioning units work by pulling in warm and humid air, cooling and drying it, and sending it back into the room while pushing heat outside. Most units double as fans, and many now include dehumidifier modes, which is something you’ll appreciate on those sticky, midsummer days when the air feels truly soupy. And, unlike central air, a window air conditioner can run on a generator during a blackout. That’s a major plus in extreme climates.

The tricky part is finding a window air conditioner that actually fits your space, is easy to install, and doesn’t drive up your energy bill. We looked at a range of models with various features and specs. Some of these we’ve tested hands-on, and a few are newer standouts with great customer reviews. Continue reading to find the window air conditioners that are worth buying right now.

As someone who lives in an older home without ductwork, I’ve owned quite a few window air conditioners over the years in my never-ending quest to find the perfect unit for my house and family. Beyond this personal experience, I worked with a team of testers here at Popular Mechanics to find units on the market that feature reliable construction, notable energy efficiency, quiet operation, and exceptional functionality.

I also spoke with industry expert Kim Lincoln to make sure our recommendations check every box. She’s a third-generation HVAC expert and sales trainer at Service Experts with 25 years of experience.

For the most recent update, I added three new products. The GE 14,000-BTU Smart Window Air Conditioner is an excellent air conditioner for cooling spA/Ces up to about 700 square feet (like living rooms or some open space floors). Meanwhile, the LG ThinQ Window Air Conditioner includes the best collection of smart features I’ve seen out of a window AC.

The GE Profile ClearView sits on your windowsill, taking up just a few inches of space while preserving most of your view. This type of AC may not work well in older homes with radiators below the windows, but it’s a great option if you have the clearance space.

We love that you can still fully open the window for fresh air, which is a rare win for a window unit. This AC also uses an inverter compressor for efficient, low-noise cooling, which makes it perfect for offices and nurseries. The digital controls are simple and straightforward, and the app makes it easy to adjust settings without needing to walk over to the unit itself. Installation can be a bit of a project due to its shape and length, so plan on having an extra set of hands close by.

Full GE Profile ClearView Window Air Conditioner Review

There’s a reason my family owns several of these air conditioners: it’s a no-frills model that’s inexpensive, reliable, and well-sized for rooms up to 150 square feet (most small- to medium-sized bedrooms). My family was gifted one, and we loved it so much that we purchased more for our kids’ bedrooms because the knobs are easy to use and there are no smart features for them to mess with.

This air conditioner has a simple two-knob control system. The top knob controls the cooling setting, while the bottom knob controls fan speed, and you have the option to run the fan with or without cooling. The appliance’s thermostat cycles the air conditioner on and off to keep the temperature within range based on the temperature you set with the top knob.

The lack of smart tech means it can only be controlled from the knobs. That was a pro for us, but it may be a con for other shoppers. Still, it’s an efficient window unit that won’t hurt your wallet and its washable filter saves you money on having to buy replacements.

Full Frigidaire FFRA051WAE Window Air Conditioner Review

This Windmill AC stands out for combining energy efficiency with reliable performance and quiet operation, all of which make it especially useful in bedrooms up to 350 square feet. Its CEER rating of 15 is one of the strongest in this lineup, and the inverter design helps it maintain temperature without the hard stop-start cycling of many traditional window units.

On lower settings, our testing team found it to run subtly enough for overnight use, and we loved how the display dims automatically for better sleep. The fan alone can handle cooler evenings, while hotter days call for full cooling. The app is intuitive and truly smart, letting you adjust settings remotely and sending helpful alerts when it’s time to clean or replace the filter. Maintenance is a key factor in air conditioner longevity, so that’s a huge plus.

Similar in design to our best overall pick, this Midea window unit uses a true U shape so the window can close deeper into the body of the air conditioner. The end benefit is quieter cooling: Once it’s properly installed, the window acts as a sound barrier between the compressor outside and your room inside. That makes it a strong choice for offices up to 350 square feet, where excess noise can become an unwelcome distraction.

The U shape also means the window does not need to be all the way closed—you can lift the window midway up the body of the unit, and let in air from the outside without uninstalling the entire air conditioner. The biggest issue with this option is that it requires a more skilled hand when installing it, with many customers reporting difficulty doing it themselves.

We’ve been using this beast of an AC to cool the entire first floor of our home with great success for a few summers now. It’s a solid pick for larger rooms up to 700 square feet, per the unit’s specifications, which is about the total square footage of our first-floor foyer, dining room, living room, kitchen, and pantry. Depending on your home’s layout and airflow, it’s hard to guarantee it will successfully and sufficiently cool multiple spaces, but it packs serious power for big rooms, too. That said, it’s noisier than other models, so take that into consideration.

While we didn’t need smart features, it’s nice that it connects to Wi-Fi so you can control settings from your phone (or with the included remote), and the interface is straightforward. The unit is designed with energy efficiency in mind, which helps to keep operating costs reasonable for its size. Installation is fairly standard with the included kit, though the unit is heavy, so you’ll want an extra set of hands. It’s likely you’ll need a support bracket, too.

Overall, this is a dependable option for cooling bigger living spaces without overcomplicating things or having to install a mini-split.

If you need an AC that can bring down the temperature quickly in a medium-sized room, take a look at this model. This smart GE unit impressed our team with speed, cooling a 100-square-foot room from 85 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit in about 15 minutes, and it’s rated for spaces up to 350 square feet. That powerful fan helps move cool air farther into the room, so it’s a good fit if you want quick relief without jumping up to an oversized unit that will drive up energy costs for no reason.

The standout feature here (and the reason for that great performance) is the powerful fan, which kept air moving even when full cooling wasn’t necessary. We love the unit’s eco mode, which cycles the compressor and fan to maintain temperature without overworking the unit. We found the installation to be manageable, but easier with two people. We love that GE includes insulation, though you may need to purchase some additional products to create a perfect seal depending on your window. The main drawback is the app, which was difficult to connect to, despite troubleshooting. Customer service at GE is great, though, and the one-year warranty gives peace of mind.

Read Full GE 8,000 BTU Air Conditioner Review

This LG 6,000 BTU unit is a strong small-space pick that adds genuinely useful smart features without overcomplicating things. It’s designed for rooms up to about 250 square feet, making it a better option for bedrooms and home offices than larger living areas.

It pairs easily with LG’s ThinQ app, so you can adjust temperature, fan speed, and schedules from your phone (or with Alexa or Google Assistant). While it’s easy to find an app-controlled window AC these days, this one stands out from the pack a bit. LG has a deeper smart-home ecosystem than most brands manufacturing window ACs, and this model brings that app control, voice-assistant compatibility, scheduling, energy-saver mode, and filter alerts to rooms up to 250 square feet. Customers find the cooling performance is consistent, and the unit includes practical touches like a filter alert and energy saver mode. It’s not the quietest or most powerful option out there, but it balances size, features, and price well for a smart-enabled window AC.

Air conditioners are rated in British thermal units (BTUs), which indicate how much space they can effectively cool. A unit that’s too small will run constantly and never quite get there, but one that’s too large will cool too quickly without removing enough humidity. This leaves the room feeling clammy and uncomfortable.

That’s why several of our superlatives are organized around room size and use case, rather than just standout features. A 5,000-BTU unit may be a smart pick for a small bedroom, dorm room, or compact home office, while an 8,000-BTU model is better suited to a medium-size room where faster cooling and stronger air movement matter. Larger living rooms, open layouts, or rooms with high ceilings may need 10,000 BTUs or more. As a loose rule of thumb, small bedrooms may need around 5,000 to 8,000 BTUs, while larger living areas can require 10,000 BTUs or more. Lincoln says the most common issue is choosing a unit that is too small.

“A window unit may be able to knock down the temperature right near the unit, but that doesn’t mean it’s doing a good job across the full area,” says Lincoln. “In oversized rooms or open floor plans, I see units run nearly nonstop while still leaving parts of the space warm and damp.” She says that’s when customers note a room feels cool but clammy. “The system may be lowering temperature near the unit, but it isn’t really winning the humidity battle across the space.”

This also explains why a powerful fan, efficient compressor, or smart app only matters if it supports the way you’ll actually use the A/C. A stronger fan is most helpful when it moves cool air across a medium or large room, while an efficient inverter unit is especially useful in bedrooms or offices where the AC may run for long stretches. Smart controls are most valuable when they make daily use easier, whether that means scheduling, remote adjustments, energy tracking, or filter reminders.

Before you buy, measure your window—twice. Window units are designed for specific opening widths and heights, and some, like casement or sliding windows, require specialized models. Even with careful planning, you may strike out at first.

“Not every window unit fits every window well, even when the box says it should,” says Lincoln. “Consumers need to look at more than width. The window style, the sash opening, the weight of the unit, and the need for support all matter.” A window unit should be level side-to-side and pitched slightly outward so condensed water drains out of the house—not into your room.

It’s important to consider the unit’s weight, too. Larger units may require a bracket or homemade support to avoid strain and damage to the window and air conditioner.

CEER stands for Combined Energy Efficiency Ratio, and it tells you how efficiently a unit uses electricity over time, not just when it’s actively cooling. Older ratings like EER measure efficiency only while the compressor is running. CEER goes a step further by also factoring in energy used when the unit is idle, like when it’s on standby or cycling on and off throughout the day.

Efficient units use less electricity to deliver the same cooling power, which matters if you’re running the A/C daily through peak summer. Features like programmable timers, eco modes, and inverter technology can further reduce energy use.

When it comes to energy efficiency, Lincoln says it’s just as much about the rating as it is about how you install the unit—specifically how well-sealed the gaps are.

“The best sealing materials are simple, cheap, and worth the effort,” says Lincoln. Foam weatherstripping, rope caulk, and other similar materials can go a long way. “I’ve seen homeowners blame the A/C when the real issue was a half-inch gap letting hot, wet air pour in all afternoon. Sealing is not just about stopping heat. It’s about stopping humidity. And in summer comfort, that distinction matters.”

If you’re used to old-school window units, you’re familiar with the buzz and crackle as they cool. Thankfully, advancements in technology have resolved that issue a bit. Not all A/Cs are created equal when it comes to sound, though. “Traditional window units tend to be louder because they cycle on and off more abruptly,” shares Lincoln. She says inverter models are often better for bedrooms and offices. An inverter unit works more like a dimmer switch than an on/off switch. Instead of turning the AC off, it slows down once it reaches your desired temperature and maintains it by running at a lower, steady speed. “The difference between a hard compressor kick and a steadier low hum is noticeable when you live with it every night.” We’ve noted this feature on the units we reviewed when applicable.

Check the decibel (dB) rating, too. Units in the low 40s are considered quiet, while anything pushing 60 dB or higher can be disruptive, especially at night.

Modern air conditioners do more than just cool. Remote controls, WiFi connectivity, and app integration let you adjust settings from anywhere. Some units include dehumidifier modes, sleep settings, or directional airflow controls that improve comfort without cranking the temperature.

Lincoln says that the “extras” worth paying for don’t often top the specs list, though. “The features worth paying for aren’t always the flashy ones. A lot of people get distracted by phone apps and forget the basics,” she says of most consumers. “The extra features I’d actually pay attention to are variable-speed operation, a true dry mode if you live in a humid climate, auto-restart after a power outage, and a thermostat or sensor that’s actually useful for where people sit or sleep.”

“Window units can be efficient, but only if the install is right,” says our expert Kim Lincoln. “A poorly sealed window AC is basically paying to cool the air around the leak.”

With the right setup, though, window air conditioners can be surprisingly efficient — especially compared to cooling an entire home with central air. Window units give you the option of cooling only the rooms you need at that time.

The key is choosing the right size and looking for models with strong CEER ratings or Energy Star certification. Features like eco mode, programmable timers, and inverter compressors can further reduce energy use by preventing the unit from constantly running at full power.

BTUs measure cooling power, and getting this right is critical. As a baseline, you’ll need about 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. For example, a 150-square-foot room typically calls for a 5,000–6,000 BTU unit. You should also factor in real-world conditions: increase capacity for sunny rooms, kitchens, or higher ceilings, and scale down slightly for shaded spaces.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close.” Be careful about over-purchasing power, though. That doesn’t mean your room will be cooler. Oversizing can lead to quick cooling without proper dehumidification, while undersizing can leave the unit running constantly.

“This is the least glamorous advice and still one of the most important,” says Lincoln. “Clean filters are still one of the biggest performance factors. For window units, the filter should be checked regularly and cleaned about once a month during heavy cooling season, sometimes more often if the home has pets, dust, smoke, renovation debris, or high traffic.”

Most manufacturer specs recommend cleaning the filter every two to four weeks during periods of heavy use, as well. A clogged filter restricts airflow, which can reduce efficiency and force the unit to work harder. The good news is that most window AC filters are washable—just remove, rinse, let dry, and reinstall. Keeping the filter clean helps maintain strong airflow, improves cooling performance, and can extend the lifespan of the unit. If your AC does not have a washable filter, Lincoln recommends keeping a spare on hand. If your AC does not have smart features or a filter reminder, it’s clutch to add this task to your personal calendar so it is not neglected.

#6393. Most of the deep ocean food supply in the Gulf of Mexico suddenly vanished, and most scientists blame the Deepwater Horizon oil spill

Deep-sea fish, krill and squid in the Gulf of Mexico fell 60 to 85 percent after 2011, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is the leading suspect.

Marine biologists have always assumed the deep ocean is the safest and most stable ecosystem on the planet. Because it is so vast and isolated from human life, they believed it was practically impossible to destroy.

Unfortunately, a massive die-off in the Gulf of Mexico just proved that assumption is dangerously incorrect.

Between 2011 and 2015, the fish, shrimp, krill and squid living in the dark water below about 650 feet (200 meters) lost 60 to 85 percent of their numbers. Surveys through 2023 have not found them coming back.

The crash shows up in two records. One is the nets that scientists have towed through the same patch of ocean in the Gulf of Mexico for 13 years. The other is ship sonar, whose echoes come back weaker when fewer animals are swimming below.

Nothing in the water itself, not temperature, oxygen or food, changed in step with it. The one event that did line up in time was the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. The authors consider this the most likely explanation.

Tracey Sutton of Nova Southeastern University led the work, with colleagues at Florida International University, the University of South Florida and NOAA.

The paper is careful about what it can show. The spill’s role is inferred from timing and from the absence of any natural driver, not from an experiment.

The record begins in January 2011, three months after the well was sealed. A nine-month campaign towed a net through a grid of 46 stations across the northern Gulf of Mexico. That first campaign is the baseline against which everything since has been measured.

The same net, with six separate bags that open and close on command, was towed again on nine shorter cruises between 2015 and 2023.

Each tow sampled from the surface down to 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) in five depth bands, at noon and again at midnight.

Towing twice a day matters, because most of these animals rise thousands of feet toward the surface every night to feed and sink again at dawn.

Only samples from the Gulf of Mexico’s own water mass were compared, since the Loop Current, which enters from the south, carries fewer animals and would have muddied the count.

Fish numbers per unit of water dropped 63.5 percent between 2011 and the later cruises. Shrimp and krill together dropped 62 percent, and small squid and their relatives dropped 59.7 percent.

The groups that feed almost everything else fell hardest. Krill dropped 72.8 percent and lanternfish 62.9 percent. Bristlemouths, tiny fish that may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth, dropped 69 percent.

The sonar agreed. Sound bouncing back from the top 650 feet (200 meters) at night, when the migrators are up feeding, was 40 percent weaker after 2011.

A drop that size over three and a half years is bigger than any change recorded over 60 years in the California Current. That is the only other long-running count of deep-sea fish.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sutton said the fall itself is not the part that surprised him most. “The slow recovery is the most surprising finding, with the realization that this downward shift may be irreversible,” he said.

And the dense swarms that predators depend on nearly disappeared. Across 134 full-column tows in the whole series, only one catch after the decline held more fish than the leanest catch of 2011.

A crowd that shrinks fast can lose genetic variety, so the team sequenced three common lanternfish species collected between 2011 and 2023, the longest such record for any deep-sea animal.

Two of the three showed it. In one species, a standard measure of genetic variety fell about 11 percent between 2011 and 2016, then recovered partway by 2023. A second species followed the same path a few years later. The third showed no clear trend.

The same tows kept adding to the list of what lives down there. Sutton told Earth.com that the deep interior holds more kinds of animals than any other part of the Gulf of Mexico, coral reefs included.

His team has recorded almost 200 fish species there for the first time since the work began, he said. That is about one in every nine fish species now known from the Gulf.

“Our knowledge of what lives in the deep ocean is incredibly poor,” he said, “even in the best-studied systems in the world, like the Gulf.”

The authors checked their own methods first. The same net, the same crew and the same analysis ran across every year, so a change in gear can’t explain the drop.

Water temperature in the twilight zone from 650 to 2,000 feet (200 to 600 meters) barely moved from year to year, and the deep Gulf stayed well supplied with oxygen. The plankton these animals eat didn’t thin out either; in 2013, mid-decline, it was above average.

So the authors turned to the spill. The Deepwater Horizon blowout on April 20, 2010 released up to 4.9 million barrels of oil over 87 days.

Crews pumped 770,000 gallons (2.9 million liters) of chemical dispersant into the plume at the wellhead, 4,900 feet down.

Oil residues turned up in the eggs of deep-sea fish and the tissues of squid at least six years later, at concentrations known to kill or weaken fish.

The paper does not test oil on these animals directly. It argues from the sequence of events and from what oil did elsewhere. For example, herring in Prince William Sound collapsed four years after the Exxon Valdez spill and have still not recovered.

The Gulf’s deep-feeding whales eat these animals, and their numbers have been falling too. Long-term counts show Gervais’ beaked whales down 83.4 percent since the spill, and sperm whales down 31 percent. This is more than the spill’s own mortality models predicted.

Tagged sperm whales are now roaming the Gulf instead of feeding in their usual predictable spots.

Endangered Rice’s whales have been recorded feeding near the bottom, often without success. In addition, researchers at sea report seeing thin whales, while stranded ones are often described as emaciated.

Sutton said 27 of the 28 whale and dolphin species known from the Gulf live in the open ocean, and nearly all of them eat the animals his team counted. Less prey means fewer marine mammals, he said, “and those that are there may be less fit.”

Bluefin and yellowfin tuna, swordfish, marlin, sailfish and sharks feed on the same animals, he said. So do seabirds that hunt lanternfish at night, including some endangered species.

These animals also run what scientists call the biological pump, the sinking of carbon from the surface into the deep ocean. “That function affects every person on the planet.”

One obvious objection is that the 2011 baseline was a single, nine-month campaign, run just after the spill. The team’s answer is that counts from the 1980s and 1990s at one eastern Gulf station look like 2011, not like anything since.

The authors wrote that the deep Gulf is now in “a sustained, low-abundance state” for which the recovery time, “if even possible, remains unknown.”

Asked by Earth.com what a recovery would take, Sutton used the researchers’ name for that dark, open water, the deep-pelagic ocean.

“We do not have the capacity to restore the deep-pelagic ocean directly, so the best we can do is give the system time and not make it worse with more pollution,” he said.

Whether the deep Gulf is coming back at all is the open question, and the same grid of stations is where an answer would first show up.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6392. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

#6391. The true power of humans and AI working together as a team is being heavily underestimated right now

A reanalysis of 74 human-AI studies finds people and AI did best together when AI explanations came with feedback that let humans learn.

A person with a good AI assistant should beat either one working alone. Two years ago a tally of 74 experiments said otherwise: on average, the human-AI pair did worse than whichever partner was better by itself.

A new recount of those same experiments says they left out something that people need in order to get good at anything – finding out whether they were right.

Only 10 of the 74 studies ever told participants the correct answer after a decision. In the few that did, and that also let the AI explain itself, the pair tended to come out ahead.

Julian Berger and Stefan Herzog of the Center for Adaptive Rationality at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin led the reanalysis. Colleagues at the University of Copenhagen and elsewhere in Europe joined them.

They didn’t run new experiments. They went back through every study in the 2024 review and coded what each one had let its participants learn.

“Learning effects in human-machine interaction remain virtually unexplored,” Berger said.

The 2024 review, published in Nature Human Behaviour, pooled studies in which people worked with an AI system on tasks such as sorting images, predicting house prices, or writing code.

Across 370 experimental conditions, the human-AI pair scored below the stronger partner on average.

The pair came out ahead only when the human was already better than the AI. When the AI was the stronger one, the pair did worse than the AI by itself. Neither the AI’s stated confidence nor its explanations changed that.

Berger’s team found that the typical study was a single session, with no practice trials, a median of 30 decisions, and no word on whether any of them was correct.

Only 10 studies, 14 percent of the 74, included a condition with outcome feedback. Just three of those looked at whether people’s use of the AI changed over the trials, and none varied feedback on purpose.

Feedback matters because it is how a person learns when to trust an AI assistant and when to overrule it. Without it, a participant who sees the AI’s answer has no way of telling whether the AI, or they themselves, tend to be right.

The team re-ran the comparison, splitting the 370 conditions by whether people got feedback. With feedback, the pair’s edge over the better partner was slightly positive. Without it, slightly negative.

By the team’s statistics there was an 84 percent probability the gap ran that way, which isn’t enough to be sure of. The team saw a clearer result once it sorted the conditions by AI explanations too.

In the 24 conditions where people got both an explanation of the AI’s reasoning and feedback on the outcome, the pair tended to outperform the better partner alone.

In the 148 conditions with explanations but no feedback, the pair did clearly worse. Without explanations, feedback made no reliable difference either way.

The authors’ reading is that an explanation helps mainly when a person can check it against results and learn how far to trust it.

Because no study varied feedback within an experiment, the team could only compare studies with it against studies without it. Other features of those studies could explain the differences.

In 12 further models that added each of the original review’s other factors, the direction held. Still, they wrote, experiments that switch feedback on and off are needed before anyone can call it a cause.

Most studies also reported only average performance across all trials, which hides any improvement late in a session.

In the three studies with trial-by-trial data, people learned to go along with an AI that was outperforming them when the task gave them something to learn from.

The authors wrote that their estimate may, therefore, understate how much learning helps.

Whether any of this carries over to chatbots is open. Herzog said a conversation with a chatbot could make tailored feedback and explanations easier to deliver.

“But for that to happen, people also need to find out what is actually correct; a chatbot’s answers can be wrong and do not constitute independent feedback,” he said.

He added a second worry. “At the same time, new risks arise from cognitive ‘offloading’ – that is, delegating mental work to AI. In the medium and long term, this could jeopardize learning success or even lead to loss of skills.”

The team called for experiments that vary feedback and the task itself, and for sharing trial-level data so that learning can be measured directly.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Archaeologists have discovered thousands of stone artifacts in Saudi Arabia, some of which suggest people were using poison-tipped stone tools to hunt large game 125,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have found what may be the world's oldest poisoned weapons at a 125,000-year-old site on an ancient lakeshore in Saudi Arabia. The stone tools, which were likely used to hunt large animals, had traces of residue from a poisonous tree historically used for its toxins.

"At 125,000 years old, these would be substantially older than the poisoned arrowheads recently identified in South Africa, which date to around 60,000 years ago," study co-author Chris Clarkson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany and Griffith University in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "But we haven't demonstrated exactly how the poison was prepared or whether it was effective. So I'd describe these as potentially the oldest evidence for poisoned hunting weapons, rather than an unequivocally established first."

In the new study, published Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Science, researchers investigated a 125,000-year-old site in southern Saudi Arabia known as 'Uruq Aljelibah, which means "sand dunes of a watering hole," study co-author Frans van Buchem, a geologist at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia, told Live Science.

Today, the area is "hot, extremely dry, with extensive sand dunes," Clarkson said, located as it is within the Empty Quarter — one of the hottest, driest deserts on Earth. But the scientists found the site was once home to a freshwater lake measuring about 130 square miles (340 square kilometers) and up to 95 feet (29 meters) deep. Fossils there suggest it once supported a rich diversity of flora and fauna, including hippopotamuses, buffalo, ostriches, camels, gazelles, oryx, palms, reeds, trees and shrubs, which early modern humans likely exploited for food and other resources.

"The idea of hippopotamuses and enormous buffalo living around a lake in what is now the Empty Quarter really brings home just how dramatically these landscapes, and global climates, have changed," Clarkson said.

Saudi Arabia is a desert today, but it used to be a lush landscape.

The archaeologists discovered more than 5,500 stone artifacts at the site, along with extraordinarily preserved traces of plant materials, such as fibers, resins and wood. Several of these artifacts were stone points that showed impact damage consistent with hunting large animals, and a microscopic analysis revealed traces of animal tissue near the point tips. The distribution of the stone tools closely matched clusters of animal bones, suggesting that the lakeshore was a focal point for hunting and processing game, according to the study.

"At most Paleolithic sites, we're lucky if we get the stone tools and perhaps a few animal bones," Clarkson said. "Here we can actually begin to reconstruct what those tools were doing and what other materials people were combining with them."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers found that people may have hunted animals with poison-tipped tools. Several stone points had chemical residues linked with the arrow poison tree (Acokanthera schimperi), which is known historically for its toxins and is native to eastern and central Africa and southern Arabia. African hunters have coated spear tips and arrowheads with extracts from this plant to paralyze or kill game.

It remains unclear how hunters who poisoned their targets might have avoided poisoning themselves upon eating the game.

"The effects of a poison depend on the substance, the dose and how it enters the body," Clarkson said. "A poison introduced directly into a wound doesn't necessarily behave in the same way when swallowed." Hunters throughout history "are known to sometimes remove the meat around the wound before eating the rest of the animal," he added.

These findings emphasize how researchers have often underestimated the technological complexity of early human populations, because so much of what they made was organic and has simply disappeared," Clarkson said. "These weren't just people knocking stone flakes off cores," Clarkson noted. "They were combining stone with wood, plant fibers, resins and potentially toxic substances to make complex tools and weapons."

To have so much evidence for how people were making and using tools in a site like this "is remarkable," Eleanor Scerri, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany who did not take part in this research, told Live Science in an email. "This goes from both the micro-scale, in finding traces of how people hafted spear tips, for instance, up to the bigger scale of the whole site and the very convincing spatial relationship between hunting-related tools and the bones of animals such as hippos."

Sites in Arabia that possess both stone tools and animal bones are rare, Jeffrey Rose, a Paleolithic archaeologist at the University of Algarve in Portugal who did not participate in this study, told Live Science in an email. "This one has thousands of artifacts on an old lakeshore alongside hippo, buffalo and ostrich, and some of the flakes fit back together, so the tools were made on the spot," he said. "It's valuable new data."

The Arabian Peninsula sits between Africa and the rest of Asia and was a major corridor for humans as they dispersed across the world. Recurring spans of increased rainfall could have made its otherwise hostile landscapes more habitable in the past. However, the hot desert that now covers much of Arabia has made it difficult for scientists to excavate many details about this vital bridge during this critical point in human history.

The researchers did not unearth any human remains. Still, they suspect the site most likely belonged to modern humans (our species, Homo sapiens), as opposed to a different human species.

"We know that H. sapiens had already expanded out of Africa and were present in Southwest Asia during this period," Clarkson said. "The age of the site fits with those early movements."

These findings add to growing evidence that wetter intervals in Arabia created migration corridors between Africa and Asia and supported productive habitats capable of sustaining repeated human occupation.

"What our site shows is that people weren't necessarily just passing through these environments," Clarkson said. "They were exploiting them in quite sophisticated ways, using a range of technologies and resources."

But Rose cautioned that all of the stone artifacts found in this study were collected from the surface. "Not one was excavated from the layers that were dated," he said. "The 125,000-year date belongs to the lake, not to the tools. For the tools, it is only a maximum age." Future research at the site should look for stone artifacts sealed in lake beds. "That's hard in Arabia, where wind has stripped most sites down to surface scatters, but it can be done," Rose said.

Clarkson agrees that further work is needed. "I'd really like to keep going back to this site to find more fossils, both animals as well as hopefully human fossils," Clarkson said. "I'd also really like to push the chemical and functional analyses further, particularly the evidence for toxic plant compounds. It would be fascinating to determine exactly which substances were being used, how they might have been prepared and whether they were deliberately applied to hunting weapons."

Future research focusing on the ancient lake margins may reveal more information. "There must be other places where people were living and carrying out activities, and some may preserve better stratified archaeological deposits," Clarkson said.

But the combination of discoveries at this site is amazing, the researchers said.

"I've spent much of my career studying stone tools, and one of the great frustrations is that we're usually only looking at the small fraction of ancient technology that survives," Clarkson said. "Here we have a chance to see much more of the complete technological system."

Clarkson, C., Price, G.J., Kalifi, A., Losi, G., Matheson, C., Al-Jibreen, F., Alsharekh, A.M., Armitage, S.J., Blilou, I., Boivin, N., Breeze, P.S., Drake, N., Duval, M., Gradwell, S., Groucutt, H.W., Guagnin, M., Guzmán, J., Hapiot, L., Martínez-Pillado, V., … van Buchem, F. (2026). Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore. Science. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aef9342

#6389. Staying social may keep an older mind sharp, but not every kind of activity counts

Among social activities older adults join, volunteering and sports clubs were linked to better memory in 24 countries. Church groups were not.

Older adults who volunteer or belong to a sports club tend to do better on memory and thinking tests than people who join nothing. The gap grows with each extra kind of social activity they take on.

The benefit didn’t show up evenly, though. Volunteering and sports clubs were linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline in all five national surveys studied. Church groups and political groups were not consistently linked to any gain.

Behind the pattern are the records of nearly 58,000 people in 24 countries, followed for about six years. The authors describe it as the first analysis to pool five national aging surveys to understand the impact of social connection.

Jiahong Sun of Guangdong Medical University and Bo Xi of Shandong University led the work with first author Yuedong Wang. It’s an observational study, so it can show that joiners scored higher, not that joining caused the higher scores.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sun said the practical message is about variety and sticking with it. “A practical step would be to take part in a few sustainable activities, ideally including three or more types of social engagement,” he said.

Social activities, he suggested, might include volunteering, joining a sports club, attending a training course or spending meaningful time caring for children..

The findings of earlier studies on the effect of social engagement disagreed with each other.

The Rush Memory and Aging Project linked higher social engagement to a five-year delay in the onset of cognitive impairment. A Dutch study of about 2,000 people found no link.

The authors suspected small samples, under 3,000 people, and inconsistent ways of measuring social life.

So Wang’s team pooled five long-running surveys of people in middle age and beyond. Three of them are the Health and Retirement Study in the United States, the English Longitudinal Study of Aging, and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study.

The Mexican Health and Aging Study and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe complete the set.

The European survey alone supplied almost half of the 57,793 participants. Median ages ran from 57 in the Chinese survey to 73 in the American one.

Each survey asked people whether they had taken part in social groups over the past month or the past year.

Memory was tested by having people recall a short list of words, right away and again later. Thinking was tested with tasks like counting backward from 100 by sevens or naming as many animals as possible in one minute.

Because the tests differed, the researchers converted every score onto one common scale, so a result from Mexico could be compared with one from England.

On that scale, people who took part in at least one social activity scored higher than people who took part in none, in all five surveys.

Each added kind of activity came with a higher score. People who kept up three or more scored more than twice as far above the inactive group as people with just one activity did.

The three-or-more group’s advantage also grew over time. Their scores improved a little faster each year than the inactive group’s did, and that extra yearly gain showed up on the memory test.

On the thinking tasks, the yearly difference was too small to separate from chance.

What the study measured was test scores, not dementia diagnoses. The authors described the trend as a dose-response pattern: more kinds of social contact, higher scores.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him about which activities helped, Sun pointed to two that showed the same link everywhere and several that didn’t.

Volunteering and sports club membership were linked to better cognitive scores in all five surveys. Attending training courses and caring for children were linked to faster yearly gains.

Political groups, community groups, church groups, and religious groups showed no consistent link across the surveys.

“This does not mean that these activities are harmful or ineffective; their associations may depend on the social and cultural context in which they occur,” Sun said.

Why would an active social life protect thinking? The authors offered three possibilities. Activities that demand attention may keep brain connections in use. This idea is often summed up as “use it or lose it.”

Social contact may add to the mental reserve that education builds up over a lifetime. And meaningful activity may lower chronic stress, which harms the brain region that handles memory.

The association was not the same for everyone. Sun said it appeared stronger among women, adults aged 60 or older, people with at least a high school education, and people without depressive symptoms.

It was also stronger among people who lived alone, were of normal weight, or lived in rural areas.

Two more groups that made the list puzzled the authors: current smokers and people who drank alcohol.

One possibility they raised is that smokers and drinkers may do their socializing in organized groups, the kind that keep a mind busy. They called that reading speculative and the whole set of subgroup results exploratory.

For people over 60, the authors’ explanation is plainer. After retirement, people have more free time for groups.

People were asked about their social activities once, at the start. The analysis assumed those habits held for the next six years., but this was not checked.

The thinking tests also differed from country to country, so a score in China and a score in England don’t measure exactly the same skill.

And people who were already sharper may have been the ones who joined clubs in the first place, which would make the clubs look better than they are.

The analysis adjusted for age, education, depression, loneliness, and several other factors, but the authors wrote that other differences between joiners and non-joiners could still explain part of the gap.

Dementia is the stake behind all of this. In 2019, about 57 million people were living with it, and the authors cited projections of nearly 153 million by 2050.

With no effective treatment available, they wrote, finding risk factors that people can change is a public health priority.

The study counted how many kinds of activity a person did. It didn’t ask whether they enjoyed them, led them, or how often they went.

“Our next steps are to examine not only the number of social activities, but also their quality, purpose, level of personal involvement and emotional experience,” Sun told Earth.com.

He added that future research should also test whether programs that get older adults into sustained social activity actually improve their cognitive health.

Until a study like that runs, the evidence is a pattern across six years and 24 countries. Whether joining is what makes the difference, or whether sharper people are the ones joining, remains an unanswered question.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.
