#6372. Watching a fight may change the brain before the first punch

Male mice learned fighting behaviors by watching others, with brain changes resembling those caused by direct fighting experience.

More than 60 years ago, Albert Bandura showed young children an adult behaving aggressively toward an inflatable doll, and the children went on to behave that way themselves.

Thanks in part to those Bobo doll studies, psychologists treat watching as a form of social learning.

Male mice pick something up from watching, too.

Males that only watched other males fight, and never once joined in, walked into their own first fight acting like animals that had been fighting for eight days.

Watching moved them partway toward experience without any of the risk that comes with it. Their brains had shifted in the same direction as the fighters’ brains, though not as far.

Annegret Falkner and her lab at Princeton sorted male mice into three groups and trained each group for eight days straight, three sessions a day.

The fighters got a smaller, submissive mouse dropped into their own cage for nine minutes at a time. Every session was an easy win.

Observers sat in a clear-walled compartment about 4 by 5 by 7 inches (10 by 13 by 17 cm). The team set it on top of another mouse’s cage, and that mouse fought below.

Cutouts in the barrier let the smell and the sound through. There was no way down.

A third group spent the same minutes with a toy mouse and saw no fighting at all.

Day nine brought the same test for everyone. Each mouse faced three back-to-back rounds of four to five minutes, in its own cage, against an undefeated male with real fighting experience.

Across those rounds, the three groups spent roughly the same amount of time in conflict. What changed was who started it.

Fighters and observers both delivered more attacks that drew no response, and both got going sooner than the toy group. They were also attacked less often. The toy-exposed mice did more fleeing.

Watching changed how the observers approached a fight, even though the groups spent similar amounts of time in conflict.

It gave them the timing and the readiness of a trained fighter without raising how much they fought.

The researchers tracked 15 points on each animal’s body, nose to tail tip, in every video frame.

Then they let software sort the footage into 13 recurring behaviors with no human labels attached.

Observers and fighters spent more of the hard fight in the tight, close-quarters postures that come right before an attack, and less of it hanging back.

The same lab had already tied those proactive postures to resilience in a 2022 study. The order of the behaviors lined up too.

The work was led by Jorge Iravedra-García, a postdoctoral researcher.

“Not only are they emulating some of these behaviors, but the way that they move between these behaviors is also quite similar,” said Iravedra-García.

“When you compute the transitions from aggression behavior one to investigation behavior two, experienced animals behave very similarly to observers in those situations as well.”

A fourth group of five mice watched other males for the same eight days, but those males were only being social. No fighting. In the hard fight, this group behaved more like the toy group than like the observers.

Watching other mice wasn’t the ingredient. Watching them fight was.

The observers also paid close attention, and the team could measure it. A program sorted every moment of video into one of seven behaviors, from grooming to pressing against the barrier with the head turned toward the slits.

That last one, attention, took up more of each session as the eight days went by.

“The observing mice don’t care so much when the fighting animals were just walking around and interacting,” Falkner said. “But we see them orient and attend once attacks start.”

While all of this went on, the team was recording from 12 brain regions at once in every animal.

Two colors did the work. Cells that excite their neighbors were engineered to shine green when active, and cells that quiet their neighbors to shine red.

Twelve optical fibers, each about eight thousandths of an inch across (0.2 mm), carried the light back out.

The moment an attack started, activity rose across most of those regions in the fighters.

Observers showed much the same rise while doing nothing but sitting and looking, and the toy group showed almost none of it. In observers, the response also faded faster.

A 2023 study from Stanford University had found cells in one small spot of the hypothalamus that fire when a mouse attacks and when it watches an attack.

The Princeton team found similar activity patterns across most of the brain regions it monitored.

Dopamine told its own story. In observers, the dopamine signal tracked how fast the attacker lunged and how fast the losing mouse ran.

The watcher was taking in both animals, rather than only the winner.

“Observation’s not a replacement for experience,” Falkner said. “But it gets you part of the way there.”

Many brain cells exist to hold other cells quiet. Researchers call that inhibition, and in these mice it loosened.

In four regions tied to aggression, fighters and observers alike showed weaker activity in those quieting cells during the hard fight than the toy group did.

The excitatory side showed no group difference at all, which points at inhibition as the thing that changed.

So the team put it back. Six observers carried an engineered receptor that let a single injection switch the quieting cells back on in four regions, 30 minutes before the hard fight.

Seven more observers got the injection with no receptor to act on.

The six fought like untrained animals. They delivered fewer attacks and took more, and their behavior slid back toward the mice that had spent eight days with a toy.

The reversal provides evidence that reduced inhibition helped drive the observers’ changed fighting behavior.

Observation did not reproduce every effect of direct fighting experience.

Behaviors that involve direct physical contact changed more after real fighting than after watching, which puts a limit on what observation alone can rewrite.

Every animal in the study was male. What a female mouse takes away from watching two males fight is an open question, and Falkner’s lab is starting there.

Human research has tied exposure to violence to a higher chance of later violence, and the argument over violent media has run for decades.

These mouse experiments cannot settle how exposure to violence affects human behavior.

Falkner’s own reading is that changes like these may suit an animal living with violence and work against one that isn’t. Plenty of brain circuitry works the same way in distant species, and biologists call that conserved.

“I have a hunch that probably some of these circuit changes are conserved in mice and humans,” Falkner said.

Her lab now wants to run the whole thing backwards. The team holds a recording of what an observer’s brain does while it watches a fight.

Falkner would like to play that pattern into a mouse that has never seen one, then put that animal in a fight. That experiment hasn’t been run yet.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

#6369. Flounders reveal an unexpected way of life in a freshwater lake

Flounders in a Finnish lake appear to spend their entire lives in freshwater, raising questions about how they reproduce without the sea.

European flounders swim into river mouths to feed, and biologists have long thought they go back to the sea or to partly salty water to spawn.

In Lake Pulmanki, in the far north of Finland, most of the flounders scientists sampled had hatched in freshwater and stayed there their whole lives.

They’re the first evidence that flounders of this group can complete their life cycle without the sea.

The lake was once a fjord, a long, narrow arm of the Arctic Ocean, and it became a freshwater lake after the last ice age. Today, about 37 miles (60 km) of river separate it from the sea.

Thais Ferreira-Araújo began the work as her graduate thesis at the University of Helsinki.

It grew into a study with co-authors in Finland, Italy, Hong Kong, Portugal, and Australia, and it was published in September.

Paolo Momigliano, an associate professor at the University of Tuscia, helped supervise the thesis.

For a sea fish, coping with water that has almost no salt is one problem, and breeding in it is another.

“This is a striking finding because reproduction poses challenges that go beyond an adult fish’s ability to tolerate freshwater,” Momigliano said.

“In fishes, including flounders, salinity affects whether sperm become motile and how eggs develop and remain suspended in the water.”

Salinity is how salty the water is, and motile sperm are sperm that can swim.

Flounders were first recorded in Lake Pulmanki in the 1970s, and researchers at the time couldn’t say why they were there.

One idea was that the fish swam up from the Barents Sea, the stretch of Arctic Ocean off northern Norway and Russia. They would feed in the lake and then head back to the sea to spawn.

The other idea was that the flounders had adapted to spend their whole lives in freshwater. To tell the two ideas apart, researchers needed to know where each fish had been born.

Ferreira-Araújo’s team looked first at otoliths, small bony structures in a fish’s inner ear that help it sense balance and movement.

As an otolith grows, its chemistry keeps a record of the waters the fish has lived in.

Scientists have used the same kind of record to trace where salmon grew up and how northern pike travel between watersheds.

Researchers studying Baltic cod paired ear-bone chemistry with DNA, and Ferreira-Araújo’s team did the same.

They read the full genomes of flounders from the lake and a few sea sites, looking for stretches of DNA that matched how each fish had used fresh and salt water.

Most of the flounders from Lake Pulmanki had spent their entire lives in freshwater. So the lake’s flounders can produce new generations without any time at sea.

The rest had spent part of their lives in salt water or in brackish water, the partly salty mix found where rivers meet the sea.

Fish with different life histories therefore share one lake. Some had lived only in freshwater, while others had spent time in saltier water.

The team found another surprise in nearby fjords, where most of the flounders sampled had also been born in freshwater, a result the authors didn’t expect.

Across the genome as a whole, flounders born in freshwater and flounders born at sea were only slightly different. But 77 small DNA differences were linked to how a fish had used fresh and salt water. They were scattered over 18 chromosomes and tied to 36 genes.

The same fish tended to carry several of these differences at once, even though they were on separate chromosomes. The researchers suggested that natural selection favored certain combinations of genes.

If so, a flounder probably needs many genes working together to live in freshwater from birth, rather than a single change.

When sea fish settle in freshwater, the freshwater group often stops breeding with its relatives at sea, which is one way new species can form.

The lake’s flounders are still genetically similar to their seagoing relatives. That lets researchers look for the exact traits and genes tied to the move into freshwater.

What researchers still don’t know is how these flounders spawn in the lake at all.

Juha Merilä, a professor at the University of Hong Kong, was another of the thesis supervisors, and he named the problem the team hasn’t solved.

“The next question is how they reproduce successfully under conditions that prevent European flounder from doing so in the rest of its range,” Merilä said.

Answering that question will require studying how the sperm and eggs of these fish behave in freshwater.

The full study was published in the journal Evolution.

#6367. How doctors phrase medical advice may shape the choices people make

A study reveals how medical advice influences treatment decisions, with people interpreting words and chances of success differently.

Doctors sometimes use words instead of numbers when giving medical advice.

For example, they may say a treatment is “likely to help” without explaining exactly how likely it is to work. This leaves patients to decide what those words mean.

Positive wording such as “it is possible” may encourage someone to recommend a treatment more strongly than negative wording such as “it is not certain.”

A study involving people with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) found that some participants were influenced more by how positive or negative the words sounded, even when they had their own ideas about the chances of success.

Others focused more on how likely they thought the treatment was to work.

The work was led by Hidehito Honda of Otemon Gakuin University, together with Hirokazu Kumazaki of Nagasaki University and Kazuhiro Ueda of the University of Tokyo.

Volunteers were asked to advise a fictional friend, so no real treatment decision was at stake for anyone taking part.

Ueda, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, explained the reasoning behind the work.

“ASD is often associated with differences in communication and information processing, so we wondered if people with ASD might interpret expressions of uncertainty differently,” said Ueda.

There were reasons to expect either outcome, since earlier research had found people with autism to be less affected by some thinking biases.

A study in The Journal of Neuroscience is one example, as describing a money choice as a gain or a loss swayed people with autism less than other participants.

However, open-ended information can be difficult for people with autism.

Other research has linked autism to a dislike of unpredictable situations, as well as to a tendency to put things into either-or categories.

It was predicted that people with autism would attach more similar numbers to different phrases and that tone would have a greater influence on their choices.

To test this, Japanese versions of a task from a 1999 study were used, in which a friend with recurring migraines was considering an expensive treatment based on acupuncture.

In each version of the story, a doctor with knowledge of migraines gave an opinion on the treatment’s chances of helping.

Eight of these opinions were expressed in words (four positive phrases such as “it is likely” and four negative ones such as “there is little hope”).

The remaining three gave a numerical chance of 10%, 30% or 50%. After each opinion, volunteers rated how strongly they would recommend the treatment on a scale of one to five.

The volunteers then wrote down the chance that they thought each phrase meant, which allowed each person’s advice to be compared with that person’s own reading of the odds.

The main experiment included 48 people with autism, recruited through a support institution for people with developmental disorders. Each of these diagnoses was made by Kumazaki, a psychiatrist with more than 20 years of experience.

A comparison group was made up of 41 people without autism, while 17 other volunteers who scored high on questionnaires about autistic traits were excluded.

Later, the same tasks were also completed online by a further group of people without autism.

The first prediction was borne out, as participants with autism tended to give the phrases more similar numbers than the group without autism (a statistically significant difference).

This pattern also appeared when pairs of phrases with opposite tones were compared. In other words, a positive and a negative phrase did not necessarily mean very different chances to the person reading them.

On average, however, all three groups did something similar, in that the higher the chance they assigned to a phrase, the more strongly they recommended the treatment.

Positive wording also gave recommendations an extra lift beyond the effect of those estimates.

In the first experiment, people without autism followed their percentages more closely, although the effect of positive wording did not clearly differ between the two groups.

These averages, however, hid some differences between individuals.

Using a statistical model, the team estimated how much each volunteer relied on their own percentage and how much on the wording, before sorting people by those scores.

One group, made up mostly of people with autism, followed the positive or negative wording, and the percentages these volunteers had given made no detectable difference to their advice.

For a second group (mostly people without autism), only the percentages mattered, while a third group of people with and without autism made use of both.

“While we found that participants with ASD tended to assign more similar numerical meanings to different verbal phrases, we more importantly identified three distinct patterns of decision-making, revealing variation both within and across the groups,” Ueda said.

There was no need to guess what the doctor meant when the opinion was given as a percentage, as every volunteer received the same 10%, 30% or 50% chance.

As that number rose, every group recommended the treatment more strongly, and no clear differences were found between groups (or between the three decision styles) on these questions.

Thus, the differences turned up when volunteers had to translate words into odds for themselves. This comparison was exploratory, meaning it wasn’t among the team’s original predictions.

The study leaves open how much of the pattern came from autism itself. In the first experiment, the estimated IQ of the autism group averaged about 92, compared with about 111 in the comparison group.

The two groups also differed in age (22 on average in the autism group and 42 in the comparison group).

To narrow these gaps, the 49 online volunteers were all in their twenties, with a high school diploma or vocational degree as their highest qualification.

The online volunteers kept the phrases further apart in numerical terms than the autism group did but closer together than the original comparison group.

The ranges overlapped, and the authors thought cognitive ability might help to explain the result.

The study could not clearly separate the possible effects of autism from those of cognitive ability.

Age and gender, on the other hand, seemed unlikely explanations for the patterns.

The team also could not say why a particular person favored one way of deciding over another. Discomfort with uncertainty was one possible explanation, but it was not measured in this study.

“Even so, our findings suggest that the way we communicate uncertainty deserves more attention, especially when people make important decisions about health, education or everyday life,” said Ueda.

“We could see that even subtle differences in wording can influence people’s decisions.”

Because the experiment involved advice for an imaginary friend, it is not yet known how people might choose when their own health or money is at stake.

Future research could look at IQ and autism traits together, in situations that are closer to real decisions.

The full study was published in the journal Psychonomic Bulletin & Review.

#6366. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

A.R. Kunik, et al. The ‘‘dark magic mushroom’’ co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin. Current Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6364. Animals in the deep ocean may have less protection than scientists thought

DNA from deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf of Mexico reveals genetic warning signs that population counts alone may miss.

Deep-ocean animal populations have long been assumed to be stable and resilient, partly because their habitats are so vast.

However, a new study of lanternfishes and deep-sea shrimp in the Gulf of Mexico suggests that this assumption may not hold.

In fact, all five species in the study carried genetic signs that conservation guidelines link to a higher risk of extinction. One lanternfish lost about 8% of its genetic diversity in 12 years.

Pedro A. Peres, a marine scientist at Florida International University (FIU), led the research.

“This challenges the idea that deep-sea species are naturally more resilient because they occupy such vast environments,” said Peres.

“It shows how much we can miss when we look only at population abundance without considering their genetic diversity and long-term viability.”

Rather than counting animals, the researchers analyzed the DNA of lanternfishes and shrimp caught over more than a decade.

They looked for the measures that conservation scientists use to judge a population’s long-term prospects.

The animals were collected through a research program set up after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster. During the spill, 4 million to 4.9 million barrels of oil were released deep below the Gulf’s surface.

The DEEPEND consortium has sampled the Gulf’s open waters ever since. The authors described its dataset as the longest record of its kind for deep-sea fishes, crustaceans, and squid and their relatives.

Crews aboard the research vessel Point Sur used six nets that open and close at set depths. Together, the nets sampled water from the surface down to about 4,900 feet (1,500 meters).

The team picked five of the most numerous animals in the Gulf’s middle depths, which lie about 650 to 3,300 feet (200 to 1,000 meters) below the surface.

Three are lanternfishes (Ceratoscopelus warmingii, Diaphus dumerilii, and Lepidophanes guentheri), and two are shrimp (Phorcosergia grandis and Robustosergia robusta).

After quality checks, DNA from 486 animals collected between 2011 and 2023 went into the final analysis.

Steep population drops had already been recorded in many Gulf animals over the past 15 years (from deep-sea fishes and crustaceans to toothed whales). Still, it wasn’t clear whether the animals’ genetic diversity had fallen too.

A population can contain huge numbers of animals while maintaining far less genetic diversity than those numbers might suggest.

Geneticists estimate its effective population size – a measure of how many individuals effectively contribute genes to future generations – from DNA.

The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted by nations in Montreal in 2022, suggests using that number to judge the risk of extinction.

Under a widely used rule, a population needs an effective size above 50 to stay viable in the short term (and more than 500 over the long term).

Scientists still debate these cutoffs, and some argue for higher ones. Even so, they remain among the measures that conservation biologists rely on most.

In the Gulf, most estimates for all five species fell below 500. Each species also had estimates near or below 50 in some of the periods that were examined.

The team used three methods, each comparing how common certain gene versions were in different sampling years. All three gave similarly low results.

According to the authors, these genetic guidelines had never been used before to judge extinction risk in any deep-sea species.

Co-author Heather Bracken-Grissom is an assistant director of the Coastlines and Oceans Division at FIU’s Institute of Environment.

“Genetic diversity provides the variation populations need to adapt to changing conditions, resist disease and recover from environmental disturbances,” said Bracken-Grissom.

“When that diversity disappears, a species can also lose the ability to withstand future threats.”

The steepest losses were seen in Diaphus dumerilii. Its diversity dropped by about 11% to 13% between 2011 and 2016, depending on the measure.

The same lanternfish then partly recovered, although by 2023 its diversity was still about 8% lower than in 2011. None of the other four species lost that much.

Ceratoscopelus warmingii declined for a while before returning to its 2011 level.

The shrimp Phorcosergia grandis ended 2023 with slightly less diversity than in 2015, and the other two species barely changed.

Losses of a similar size have been recorded in threatened species elsewhere, but over much longer spans of time.

The critically endangered regent honeyeater (a bird), for instance, lost 9% of its genetic diversity between 1919 and the 2010s.

Thus, Diaphus dumerilii lost nearly as much diversity in 12 years as the honeyeater did in more than 90 years. Populations can recover after this kind of loss, the authors wrote.

Net catches, sound-based surveys, and the new genetic results all point to population crashes between 2011 and 2015, the authors wrote.

Together, these results suggest that a disturbance may have affected many parts of the ecosystem.

Diaphus dumerilii may have been especially exposed to the oil.

Many lanternfishes travel long distances up and down each day, but this one makes shorter trips, and its adults live near the seafloor.

After the spill, a plume of oil about 250 miles (400 kilometers) long remained in deep water for at least six months before later settling near the ocean floor.

Earlier research also found more contaminants in this lanternfish than in other animals sharing its waters.

However, the researchers couldn’t link the genetic changes directly to the spill, because so little data exists from before it.

Models of each species’ genetic history also estimated that all five had gone through large declines in the past.

The two methods used by the team, though, disagreed on whether those declines were slow or sudden.

“Our results suggest some deep-sea populations may have already been genetically vulnerable before the Deepwater Horizon oil spill,” said Peres.

“This has important implications for understanding the consequences of environmental disturbances. Events such as oil spills may affect populations that already have limited genetic resilience.”

To look ahead, the team built computer models from records of where each species has been found across the Atlantic. These models linked the records to ocean conditions such as temperature, saltiness, and currents.

The models were then projected to 2050 and 2100 under four climate scenarios, ranging from low to extreme greenhouse gas emissions.

For four of the five species, the models projected a less suitable Gulf. Depending on the species and scenario, the projected loss of suitable area ranged from 5.2% to 70%.

The biggest losses were projected for 2100 under high and extreme emissions.

The shrimp Phorcosergia grandis was the only species whose models pointed to a more suitable Gulf on average, though these models were the least reliable of the five.

The authors urged caution with these projections. Records of deep-sea animals are scarce, and data on conditions at the exact depths where these species live weren’t available.

Instead, conditions at the surface and the seafloor were used.

These animals can travel as much as 3,300 feet (1,000 meters) up and down in a day, so they’re exposed to both, the authors wrote.

In principle, animals arriving from nearby waters could bring back some of the lost genetic diversity. However, few studies have compared these species across regions.

As a result, little is known about how much the Gulf’s populations mix with others.

Changes in inbreeding over the years offer indirect hints. Still, the authors wrote that their reading of those hints should be treated as speculation.

“This study serves as a wake-up call for the scientific community, highlighting the urgent need to integrate genetic monitoring into biodiversity assessments and emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring to better understand and detect changes in marine populations over time,” Peres said.

Future studies of how these populations connect could show whether animals from elsewhere are replacing some of the lost diversity.

Sampling in the Gulf is still underway, with the DEEPEND surveys funded through at least 2029.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6362. Mangroves are making a comeback on the coast of Myanmar

Landsat images reveal mangroves reclaiming former rice fields in Myanmar, offering a local view of a wider global forest recovery.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features a coastline where forests are reclaiming ground.

Along southern Myanmar, mangroves have spread into former rice fields and expanded beside waterways, adding green to places that looked noticeably more open 16 years earlier.

The paired Landsat views capture part of Palaw Township in the country’s Myeik District. Brown agricultural patches interrupt the coastal vegetation in the earlier image.

In the later view, some of those patches have become greener as trees return.

Landsat 5’s Thematic Mapper recorded the first scene on February 14, 2010. Landsat 9’s Operational Land Imager captured the second on February 2, 2026.

Together, they offer a local view of a broader change: after decades of retreat, mangrove forests have begun gaining ground globally.

South of the village of Kyauktaung, much of the apparent recovery occupies abandoned rice fields. Elsewhere along this coast, mangroves have spread into new areas.

Those two pathways matter. A forest can expand because trees return to land where they once grew, or because they establish themselves on newly available ground.

The resulting green patches may look similar from space, but they reflect different changes on the coast.

Nearby Pyin Bukyi Island has also been the setting for conservation and planting projects intended to support mangroves.

The images show a landscape where natural regeneration and human efforts can both contribute to recovery.

Myanmar’s recent gains follow substantial losses. Agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting removed mangroves across coastal areas during the 1980s and 1990s.

The country lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010.

Since then, its mangrove area has increased by about 10 percent. That represents a reversal in direction, although it has not erased the earlier decline.

The local changes fit a global pattern identified by researchers who examined Landsat observations from 1984 through 2023.

Led by environmental scientist Zhen Zhang of Tulane University, the team tracked both mangrove extent and canopy cover.

Their study, published in the journal Science, found that the global balance shifted from net loss to net gain around 2010.

Between 1984 and 2010, mangroves lost nearly 3,000 square kilometers, or 1,200 square miles. After 2010, they gained nearly 2,000 square kilometers, or 770 square miles.

The researchers also found increasing canopy cover in forests that persisted through the study period.

That distinction adds another dimension to the recovery: some existing forests were filling in as mangroves expanded elsewhere.

By 2023, global mangrove extent was approximately 0.5 percent below its level in the 1980s, with uncertainty around that estimate.

Much of the earlier loss had therefore been offset, although the global total conceals substantial differences among regions.

Mangroves occupy a shifting boundary between land and sea. In some places, rivers deliver enough sediment to build mudflats where trees can take root.

Sediment accumulation has helped mangroves expand around the Amazon River’s mouth and across parts of northern Australia. These coastal changes have supported gains there since the 1990s.

Temperature also influences where mangroves can grow.

Along the colder edges of their range, including the southeastern United States, warmer conditions and fewer freezes have allowed trees to establish themselves in previously unsuitable areas.

Globally, about two-thirds of the expansion identified by the researchers came from mangroves colonizing new areas.

Restoration and regrowth in degraded places accounted for the remaining third.

The findings show why a mangrove comeback cannot be measured simply by counting planted trees.

Natural expansion and the return of forests to previously cleared land account for much of the change.

Mangroves help protect shorelines from erosion and storm surges.

Their roots shelter fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine animals, while the ecosystems store substantial amounts of carbon.

Those benefits make the returning forests significant for coastal communities as well as wildlife. But recovery remains uneven.

Losses in the Niger Delta have contributed to declining mangrove area across West and Central Africa since 2010.

Tropical cyclones have also degraded extensive forests in North America and southern Africa.

The Myanmar images capture one encouraging part of that complicated picture. Fields have given way to trees, and stretches of coast have gained forest cover.

The larger challenge is keeping that recovery going while protecting the mangroves that remain.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

#6360. ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus

ZWO has added a new entry point to its smart telescope lineup. The Seestar S30 Plus went on sale Nov. 10 for $499 — $474 for a limited time — undercutting the S30 Pro by $200 and making it the cheapest Seestar available.

“Many people are interested in astrophotography but hesitate when they see the equipment and setup traditionally involved,” ZWO founder Sam Wen said in a press release. “With S30 Plus, we wanted to give beginners more room to explore and create without taking away the simplicity that makes Seestar easy to start with.”

Since the original S50 debuted in April 2023, the Seestar line has continued to grow, most recently with this year’s 4K S30 Pro and S50 Pro. The S30 Plus heads in the opposite direction from the Pro models — and with the original S30 reportedly discontinued, it now holds down the entry-level slot.

Effectively, the new Plus model is an S30 Pro with a few features stripped out to meet a lower price. Like the Pro, it carries two cameras: a telephoto for galaxies, nebulae, and other deep-sky targets; and a wide-angle for broad sweeps of the night sky. The telephoto camera keeps the Pro’s 1.2-inch (30 millimeters) aperture and four-element apochromatic lens, including an element of extra-low-dispersion (ED) glass.

The biggest change is to the sensors. Both of the Plus’ cameras shoot 1440×2560 images (3.7 megapixels, or roughly 2K), versus the S30 Pro’s 8.3-megapixel 4K output — still a step up from the original S30’s 2.1 megapixels. But the difference in sensor size doesn’t mean less detail — only a difference in field of view. The Plus has the same pixel size as the Pro, so zooming in on your photos reveals the same level of detail.d

RELATED: Review: ZWO Seestar S50 smart telescope

On the telephoto side, the Plus swaps the Pro’s larger Sony sensor for a 1/1.8-inch SmartSens SC485SL chip. Both have the same 2.9-micrometer pixels behind the same 160 mm lens, so the Pro’s bigger chip just spans more sky: about 4.6°, compared with the Plus’ 3°. That’s still enough to comfortably frame targets like the Pleiades star cluster and the Orion and Rosette nebulae, along with the Moon’s full disk — or the Sun’s, with the included solar filter in place.

The wide-angle camera uses the same 1/2-inch Sony IMX586 sensor as the Pro, behind a lens with identical specs (6 mm, f/1.75). But where the Pro takes in a 63° view, the Plus crops it down to the same 2K format as its telephoto sensor, covering a smaller 43.5° field — still wide enough for the Milky Way, whole constellations, star trails, and time-lapses.

The Plus does give up a few of the S30 Pro’s handier features. The Pro can run both cameras at once, stacking a nebula through the telephoto while the wide-angle captures the Milky Way and landscape around it; the Plus only shoots with one at a time. Its wide-angle camera also can’t stitch Milky Way panoramas, though a telephoto mosaic mode for larger deep-sky targets remains. And onboard storage is halved to 64 GB.

In the box, buyers get the scope, a tabletop tripod, a carrying case, a USB-C cable, and a magnetic solar filter. The 3.6-pound (1.65 kilograms) unit runs up to 6 hours on a charge and has UV/IR-cut and duo-band light-pollution filters built in.

Like every Seestar, the S30 Plus is driven entirely from a phone through the Seestar app. Users simply pair the device to their phone, let it calibrate, and then pick a target — or let the app suggest one. The S30 Plus automatically slews to the target, centers it, and begins tracking and live stacking, with the image building in detail on screen as frames accumulate.

The app can also identify and label constellations in the wide-angle view, and it can queue up automated imaging plans to run through the night. Finished shots can be tweaked and shared straight from the phone. For those who’d rather process elsewhere, the scope saves stills as JPEG and FITS files and video as MP4 and AVI.

The Seestar S30 Plus is available now for $499 through Seestar’s and ZWO’s online stores, Amazon in the U.S. and Europe, and authorized dealers worldwide. It’s now the cheapest way into the Seestar ecosystem — and owners who outgrow it can easily step up to a Pro model.

#6359. America’s power grid is falling behind as electricity demand surges

America’s electricity demand is rising, but power line construction is lagging. A new analysis examines the barriers and possible solutions.

Electricity demand in the United States is rising fast. However, the high-voltage lines needed to carry that power between regions are not being built at anything like the rate required.

Technology that can move far greater amounts of power already exists. A new analysis by energy policy experts links the shortfall to something else, namely the way decisions about power lines get made.

The analysis was written by Madeline Yozwiak and M. Granger Morgan of Carnegie Mellon University and David G. Victor of the University of California San Diego.

It is a policy paper (not an experiment) that draws upon earlier studies and reports.

Few places, the authors wrote, face as extreme a shortage as the United States. “The fundamental challenge isn’t technical, it’s jurisdictional,” the authors wrote.

“Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward.”

Across the continental United States, only about 500 miles per year of new high-voltage lines (345 kilovolts or above) have been built in the past five years.

The figure is just a tenth of the 5,000 new miles per year that studies suggest will be needed, the authors wrote, citing a Department of Energy report.

At the higher rate, the grid that links regions would triple by 2050.

Demand is rising partly because of electric vehicles, electrified heavy industry, and the rapid growth of data centers.

Wind and solar power are also variable, which means that a grid depending on it has to move more power over longer distances.

Mileage is only part of the problem, however.

Where the lines are built matters too, the authors wrote, since links between whole regions can make the power grid more reliable and lower consumer costs.

History is part of the reason. Before the 1920s, electric power was mainly a local and regional business.

States granted each utility the sole right to serve its area, and in return a state commission was given control of its prices.

The federal government played only a secondary role until the energy crisis of the 1970s, when a stronger regulator, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), was created.

FERC gradually gained authority over line planning and rates, but key elements of state oversight were left intact.

Regulated utilities own most of the transmission lines, and state regulators reward them for projects built inside their own territories.

A line that crosses state borders involves more players, triggers federal oversight, and raises arguments about which customers pay.

A utility that owns both power plants and lines can profit when limited transmission keeps prices high.

Independent developers aren’t tied to one territory. Even so, laws in 10 states give the existing utility first claim on a proposed project.

There are two upgrades that can add capacity without a new route.

The wires on an existing high-voltage line can be replaced, or the line can be converted to direct current (DC), and either can sometimes triple its capacity.

These upgrades use existing routes, where local opposition may be weaker because power lines are already in place.

Alternating current, used on most of the grid, can only be moved over short distances when the cable is buried. DC cables, however, can run underground much farther.

One example is the Champlain Hudson Power Express, a 339-mile (545-kilometer) line that was built to carry hydropower from Quebec to New York City.

Its cables are buried along transportation corridors and under Lake Champlain and the Hudson River.

Illinois bans new lines along highways and railroads, whereas laws have been passed in Michigan and Wisconsin to make such projects easier.

The authors made three proposals, and the first needs no new laws.

Under a 2005 law, the Department of Energy is allowed to name corridors of national interest, where the permitting of new power lines is simpler.

In 2021 the program was relaunched, but the corridors that had been named were canceled by the Trump administration in August 2026.

The authors called the framework solid and urged the federal agencies to create several such corridors again.

There is a role for the states as well. The laws that give existing utilities the first claim on new projects could be repealed.

In addition, more of a line’s benefits could be shared with host communities, which would reward building rather than blocking.

Texas took this approach with its Competitive Renewable Energy Zone program, in which proposals sought directly from stakeholders created a race to build.

Other nations face similar challenges, the authors wrote.

Sweden, which is rich in hydropower, rejected a link with Germany because it feared higher power prices at home.

France and Spain needed six years to reach a cost-sharing deal for an undersea link.

As a partial fix, the European Union and Australia have created joint processes for planning and building lines across member countries and states.

The second proposal is to learn from this experience. A cross-national forum, led by the national association of state utility regulators, would study what has worked abroad.

Existing comparisons of power grids, the authors wrote, tend to be too broad for lessons to move from one place to another.

The third proposal is a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission. It would be created by Congress together with the White House.

What would such a commission do? It would draft laws at the federal and state levels, assess whether the powers of FERC or other bodies should be expanded, and identify which incentives deserve public money.

However, public spending won’t be the main answer in a time of tightening budgets, the authors wrote.

Instead, bonus incentives (such as money and faster permits) could be offered to the developers who build first and to the communities that host their lines.

Private investors will ultimately decide what gets built, the authors wrote, and there will be no single national plan.

The authors did not estimate how much additional transmission construction these incentives would encourage. The commission itself remains only a proposal.

A bipartisan federal bill was also proposed recently that would, if adopted, ease permitting and reduce delays and veto points, the authors suggest.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6358. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6357. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 12: An open cluster in Perseus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

The constellation Perseus is famous for its bright Double Cluster, but these two open clusters aren’t the only groups of young stars in the Hero worth viewing. Today, let’s shift our gaze to the western portion of this constellation, near its border with Andromeda, to check out M34, a mid-5th-magnitude open cluster containing about 100 stars.

Sitting 5.2° west-northwest of 2nd-magnitude Algol (Beta [β] Persei), M34 spans about half a degree, roughly the size of the Full Moon. In physical space, astronomers believe the group spans about 14 light-years and sits 1,400 light-years away. It’s best seen under lower magnifications, such as in binoculars or small amateur scopes (4 inches or so). You’ll spot several dozen stars brighter than 12th magnitude, with its brightest suns spread throughout the cluster.

#6355. Teenage boys are spending less time outside, but what has changed?

U.S. teenage boys’ outdoor time fell from over an hour a day around 2010 to under 40 minutes by 2023, while girls’ outdoor time changed little.

Teenage boys in the United States once spent considerably more time outdoors than teenage girls. Around 2010, that gap was still clear. Since then, boys’ outdoor time has fallen sharply.

American boys aged 15 to 19 averaged more than 60 minutes a day outdoors around 2010. By 2023 they were under 40 minutes.

Girls initially spent less time outdoors, and their average changed little. By 2023, boys and girls were spending similarly limited amounts of time outside.

The analysis was led by Ewa Jarosz in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oslo.

Her co-authors were Vidar Ulset of the Norwegian School of Sport Sciences and Vegard Skirbekk, who also works at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

Time outdoors is where teenagers get their daylight and a large share of their physical activity, and the study can’t say what caused the drop, only what moved alongside it.

The numbers come from the American Time Use Survey, which the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has run since 2003.

Each person in it walks an interviewer through one full day, activity by activity, with where they were and who was with them.

The team pulled every diary from someone aged 15 to 19 between 2003 and 2023, which came to 14,235 days.

Time counted as outdoors when the diary placed the person outside away from home, or walking or cycling somewhere.

It also counted when the activity only happens outside, such as mowing a lawn, hunting or playing an outdoor sport.

Some outdoor time was missed on purpose. The survey lumps home and yard together, and it doesn’t say whether time at school was in a classroom or on a field, so neither was counted.

The team applied the same rule to every year, allowing consistent comparisons while leaving some outdoor time unmeasured.

Outdoor time for all teenagers fell over the 20 years, and the decline was concentrated among boys.

Girls’ time changed little, and the sex difference that was clear in 2010 was no longer detectable in recent years.

The steepest part of the drop for boys came after the pandemic, in both whether they went out at all and how long they stayed.

The year 2020 itself was left out of the trend lines because the survey was disrupted that year.

Some things went with more outdoor time for both sexes.

Teenagers under 16 spent more time outside than older ones, as did those in the Northeast and West and those from higher-income households.

Weekends brought longer stretches outside. Black teenagers were more likely to go out on a given day but stayed out for less time.

The team then set outdoor time beside three other ways of spending leisure: computer use and gaming, indoor exercise, and time with friends.

Smartphones were left out, because the survey didn’t measure them the same way every year and because a phone can be used outside.

Boys in the top quarter for computer leisure were less likely to go outside at all, and spent less time there when they did.

Girls showed a similar pattern, but the association was not statistically significant.

Boys who were heavy computer users spent about as much time outdoors as girls.

Time with friends ran the other way. Teenagers who spent more than the typical amount of time with a friend were more likely to be outside, boys and girls alike.

The quarter who spent the most time with friends also stayed out longest. Over the same 20 years, time with friends fell sharply for both.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jarosz said hanging out itself is in decline. It used to be low-cost and easy to arrange, she said, and now “it is crowded out by other activities.”

Could more indoor exercise have offset the loss of outdoor time? The study found no increase in indoor physical activity over the period.

Teenagers who exercised indoors were also more likely to spend time outdoors.

One kind of activity went with the other rather than replacing it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Jarosz said the decline among boys, which worries her.

Men need more physical activity than women to get the same heart benefits, she said.

Jarosz suggested that less outdoor time could also leave boys fewer opportunities for rough-and-tumble play.

The researchers noted that indoor exercise is also selective, with cost a common barrier, and that a recent pooled analysis found people enjoy it less than activity outdoors.

Each teenager appears once, on one day, so the study tracks a population rather than following any person as they grow.

The diaries also say nothing about what the outdoors looked like, so a wooded park and a parking lot count the same.

Asked what parents can do, Jarosz said habits are mostly set earlier in childhood, and that for 15- to 19-year-olds the peer group matters more than parents do.

She was careful to call that her view rather than a study finding. She pointed instead at where teenagers live.

“We know this is highly stratified, which means that it depends on your socioeconomic status what type of outdoor environment you have nearby,” Jarosz noted.

Whether the decline has bottomed out is an open question. Jarosz said outdoor time ticked up slightly in 2021 compared with 2020, by too little to count, and that she expects some recovery now that the pandemic is over.

“The decline started already around 2010 and I think the likelihood of returning to 2010 levels of outdoor time without some intervention is probably low,” she told Earth.com.

The next diaries will show whether she is right, one day at a time.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6353. Nov. 12, 2014: The Philae lander touches down on a comet

The European Space Agency’s Rosetta mission launched March 2, 2004, on a 4-billion-mile (6.4 billion kilometers) path to Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. The mission consisted of the Rosetta orbiter and the Philae lander, both designed for in-depth study of the comet. The spacecraft arrived at 67P/C-G on Aug. 6, 2014, and began orbiting the body a month later; on Nov. 12, 2014, the Philae lander descended to the comet surface. Both the spacecraft orbiting a comet and the landing on the comet’s surface were firsts in space exploration history.

Unfortunately, there were some complications with the landing: The harpoon system that was designed to hold the lander in place didn’t work, causing Philae to bounce and to float and drift above the surface. When it finally came to rest, it was in a shadowy location now known as Abydos, limiting to the sunlight its solar panels received.

Despite these challenges, Philae was able to operate for three days on battery power, and still sent back photos and data about the composition of the comet’s dust and its analysis of the body’s magnetism. (In short, the comet didn’t have a magnetic field.) Additionally, the orbiter transmitted data about water and oxygen in the tail that led to new understanding of such comets’ makeup.

#6352. ADHD is linked to higher death rates from suicide, injury and illness

People diagnosed with ADHD died at a 70% higher rate across 19 studies, and those on ADHD medication died at a lower rate, a new review finds.

Most people think of ADHD as a childhood problem, the kind of thing a kid grows out of as they become adults. But a new pooled analysis of 19 studies says it is also linked to shockingly higher death rates

Across those studies and nearly 16 million people, those diagnosed with ADHD died at a 70 percent higher rate than those without it.

The extra deaths came from suicide, from injuries and from ordinary illness alike. And in the three studies that looked, people with ADHD who took medication for it died at a lower rate than those who didn’t.

Researchers at University College London and the University of Liverpool pooled the studies on ADHD and death. Every one of them was observational. The review can show that ADHD and earlier death go together, not that one causes the other.

In an interview with Earth.com, senior author Joshua Stott, a professor in UCL’s Psychology and Language Sciences division, said doctors should take the range of causes seriously.

“Clinicians should be aware that ADHD is associated with higher mortality risk via a variety of routes including accidental death and suicide and causes likely to do with co-occurring health problems,” Stott said.

The team investigated six research databases and found 19 studies published between 2012 and 2025. Each followed people with and without ADHD, some for more than 20 years.

The studies came from the United States, Canada, Sweden, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, Finland and Denmark, and about a third of the participants were female.

Twelve of the studies reported numbers that could be combined. In that pool, the rate of death by suicide was 90 percent higher among people with ADHD.

The rate of death from injury, intentional or not, was 55 percent higher. The rate of death from natural causes was 27 percent higher.

The size of the gap varied a lot from study to study. The direction did not. Every study found more deaths in the ADHD group, which the authors read as disagreement about how much, not whether.

The authors point to several paths. Differences in impulse control, emotional regulation and risk-taking can raise the chance of injury.

ADHD often comes with depression and other mental health conditions that raise the risk of suicide. Earlier work has tied ADHD to serious transport accidents.

The deaths from illness have their own explanations. People with ADHD have higher rates of heart disease and metabolic disorders. They smoke more, have more sleep disorders, and can find it harder to keep up with treatment plans and appointments.

The authors also note that people with ADHD face more exclusion, disadvantage and stigma. Substance use, they write, can be a response to environments that offer little support.

Stott said the condition itself does not have to shorten a life. “ADHD is not by definition a life-limiting condition as the right support and treatment can help people with ADHD to live long and healthy lives.”

Three of the studies, from Taiwan, Quebec and Sweden, compared people with ADHD who took medication for it against those who did not. Pooled together, the medicated group had a 25 percent lower rate of death from any cause.

The authors treat that number with care. People who get prescriptions may differ from people who don’t in how severe their ADHD is, how easily they reach health care, and what other conditions they have.

Three studies can’t untangle that. The paper says the result should not be read as proof that ADHD medication protects against death.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him most, Stott named the potential role of medication. The team doesn’t know whether the finding is causal, he told Earth.com. But some risks, such as accidental death, may be tied to traits like impulsivity that medication can help with.

“Our findings provide early evidence to suggest that medication may play an important role in supporting the health of people with ADHD,” said first author Lucy Corrigan of the University of Liverpool.

However, she cautioned that this is based on a small number of studies so the findings are preliminary. Further research is needed to clarify this link.

Seven of the 19 studies could not be pooled. They reported their results differently or measured outcomes, such as deaths from COVID-19, that nothing else matched.

Most of the studies had more men than women, which may hide risks specific to women, who are diagnosed less often. The studies also adjusted for different things, so the pooled figures are averages across very different populations.

An earlier review of ADHD and mortality found no clear rise in deaths from natural causes. This one did, which the authors attribute to newer studies and to differences in which studies were included.

The review builds on the group’s earlier finding that adults with diagnosed ADHD have a shorter life expectancy. The authors also note that autism, which often occurs alongside ADHD, may account for part of the risk.

Whether treatment lowers the death rate, or whether treated people were simply healthier to begin with, is the open question.

Asked what it would take to answer it, Stott said the ideal would be a randomized trial with long-term follow-up. Such trials are expensive and hard to run over long time frames, he said.

The authors call for studies of women, of minoritized racial and ethnic groups, and of people who were maltreated as children, to find out who carries the highest risk. For now, Stott said, the deaths come by several routes, and the support will have to as well.

“I think it is useful to highlight that [for] people with ADHD, mortality risk was apparent across a variety of routes so it is likely that support will be needed in a number of areas to reduce this,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.
