#6261. Great Wolf Lodge Coupons: 50% Off This November

Family vacations come in all shapes and sizes, but sometimes, it’s all about the kids. That’s when places like Great Wolf Lodge come in clutch. Between the indoor water parks, arcades, and arts and crafts, they’re designed for keeping bundles of energy entertained…both kids and kids at heart. I’ve been to a Great Wolf Lodge once (in LaGrange, just outside of Atlanta) and had a ball going down those water slides and playing arcade games, even as a kid-free twenty-something.

The family resort chain has more than 20 properties across North America; most are clustered on the East Coast and in the Midwest, though there are a handful out west too. If a family vacation calls and you’re looking for ways to save on the stay, keep reading.

Great news—Great Wolf Lodge's early Black Friday sale has begun! Book by November 15 for access to room rates starting at $89 for stays taken by February 25, 2027. Browse locations here; the coupon code will be added automatically as you check out. For more short-term plans, use Great Wolf Lodge’s discount code TRIPLEFUN to take up to 40% off your total stay when staying three nights or longer within 60 days of booking. The length of stay requirements for this Great Wolf Lodge coupon mean you’ll have more time to fully experience all of the lodge activities, from the water park to the ropes course and arcade. Of note, Great Wolf Lodge Niagara is excluded from the deal.

If you’re planning a weekend trip (or a shorter mid-week trip!), use promo code MOREFUN to save 30% on two-night bookings for stays within 60 days of purchase. Special discounted rates on Great Wolf Lodge day passes are available for military members (active, retired, and veteran), teachers, fire and emergency medical service personnel, medical providers, nurses, 911 dispatchers, police, government employees, and correctional officers looking for a respite. One other reliable way to save: Join the Voyagers Club for free to earn points and exclusive members-only deals. They’ll also earn Voyagers Points for money spent at the lodge, which can be redeemed for future stays or on-site amenities.

You'll get a point for every $10 spent on bookings, package add-ons, cabanas, ancillary purchases like late checkout, and on-site spending charged to the suite, including food and retail. Points are not earned on any alcohol purchases, taxes, gratuities, fees, or on-site purchases not charged to the suite. You can check your points balance at any time in your Great Wolf profile, and redeem them by booking directly on greatwolf.com while logged into your account.

Having trouble with a promo code? There are a few things you can do to fix that. First, double check that the code is spelled correctly, with no extra spaces or typos. If all looks good, check the details of the promo code to ensure it's still active and hasn't expired. Some discount codes exclude certain locations, so make sure your booking meets any necessary criteria to qualify. If everything looks good and your Great Wolf Lodge promo code still isn't working, clear your browser's cache and give the page a refresh. When in doubt, contact the brand's customer service team for help (which varies by location).

#6260. A Wonderfully Relaxing “Afternoon Matinée” In SAS A330 Business Class

Our SAS A330-300 Business Class flight from Copenhagen to Chicago could not have been better and it really was one of the most relaxing flights I’ve had in a long time, during which I enjoyed great food and watched two excellent movies when I could not sleep.

Unless I’m flying on a plane with Starlink, I assume that the internet is not going to work onboard (especially on SAS). If it does, it is a pleasant surprise. If not, in most cases I will have already completed essential tasks so that I’m not spending my flight dreading unfinished work.

We flew home on Sunday afternoon, also a day off for me, and I decided that I’d just relax and watch some movies during the flight if I could not sleep between meals.

Lunch, by the way, was delicious. I pre-ordered “ASC” salmon with tomato vinaigrette, summer cabbage with brown butter, Jerusalem artichoke soufflé, and chive oil while Heidi pre-ordered beef with osso buco sauce, polenta cake, butter-and-thyme carrot, grilled artichoke and gremolata. We shared. Both dishes were perfect.

The appetizer and dessert were also excellent, as was the coffee:

I find the catering consistently excellent on SAS.

I did try to sleep, but could not, but that turned out to be a blessing in disguise on this flight. First I watched a Japanese movie called A Pale View of Hills, which I found riveting and very well-done. It trace the story of Etsuko and has a beautiful twist that left me profoundly moved. Highly recommended.

Meanwhile, Heidi was watching a German movie called Sound of Falling, a psychological drama spanning a century at a farmhouse in rural Germany. I then watched that while she watched the Japanese move. Wow, also excellent. Riveting and thought-provoking.

We don’t have a TV at home and I do not watch movies or anything at all unless I’m on a plane, but watching movies like this makes me think that I may be missing out…both were so well done and absolutely worth the time. I honestly could not stop thinking about either one for a couple days.

Before a landing, a delicious open-face sandwich was served with eggs and shrimp.

The flight crew was excellent and the kids were again very well-behaved, so I really don’t think it could have been a better flight. SAS does not have a cutting edge business class seat, but between my six hours of sleep on the way to Copenhagen and my restful flight on the way back, I was reminded again how much I love fly SAS Business Class and hope that I can find a way to replenish my EuroBonus account once we spend down the rest of the two million points.

I’m not sure whether I will offer a full review of this flight…I took a lot more pictures, but I’ve reviewed this product recently and little has changed. Bottom line: I do strongly recommend SAS for intercontinental travel.

#6259. Report: Google Accepts Privacy Safeguards for Spirit Data

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that the proposed sale will exclude personnel records, including medical files, results of drug and alcohol tests, performance reviews, payroll information, and grievance and arbitration filings.

Unions representing former Spirit pilots and flight attendants had objected to the inclusion of that data, noting Google’s plans to use the information to train its artificial intelligence models. The agreement reached this week resolves the unions’ concerns, the Journal said.

Google and Spirit initially planned to have an outside company “deidentify” the airline’s records. That process will still take place, though at a higher standard than Spirit intended to use, and Google will be prohibited from attempting to “reidentify” the data.

Spirit went out of business in May following a dramatic rise in jet fuel prices. The decision to auction off its internal records for use by AI was a first for the airline industry and opened up a new realm of contestation for workers and employers.

It's a question we've been diving deep into at The Points Guy this month (and something we've been debating for years now). Not only has it been harder to get upgrades and more expensive to earn status, but redemptions have gotten more expensive and watered-down benefits have made pursuing status less appealing for many of us at The Points Guy.

But not me. Despite my complaints, I'm still a fan of top-tier status and can't quit the hamster wheel, though I'm not trying for quite so many these days.

I've already requalified for World of Hyatt Globalist status this year, and I'll be able to requalify for top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status. But I will also hold lower-tier status with United MileagePlus, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program and Delta SkyMiles.

In 2027, I'll continue to hold Platinum Elite status in IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy, as well as Hilton Honors Diamond status and Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, just for carrying credit cards.

I even have top-tier status with Starbucks Rewards.

Here's the full breakdown of my elite-status plans for 2027, the credit cards I use to fast-track them, plus some tips to help you achieve your own status goals before the end of the year.

I've held top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage Executive Platinum status on and off for years now. I'm already getting closer to requalifying for 2027, and since the qualification year runs through Feb. 28, I have a few more months to work toward my goal.

So far, I've earned 148,538 Loyalty Points — the metric that AAdvantage members must accrue to earn elite status — toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required to qualify for the Executive Platinum tier. Once I hit that threshold, I'll requalify for perks like a 120% mileage bonus, Group 1 boarding, complimentary food and drinks when traveling in the main cabin and more.

Related: 5 ways to earn more American Airlines Loyalty Points before February ends

Thanks to the airline's Loyalty Point Rewards milestones, I can also hit a few more reward tiers along the way to Executive Platinum status. For example, once I hit 175,000 Loyalty Points, I can choose from a menu of valuable benefits, including two systemwide upgrade certificates.

I'm likely to choose systemwide upgrades again, but the 25,000 bonus miles and the trip credits are probably the best alternate options.

I've already used two systemwide upgrades from coach to business class on AA's transcontinental flight from San Francisco to New York and back. I also just confirmed two more upgrades for upcoming international trips, including a flight to Paris from New York and another from London back to New York.

Holding the (see rates and fees) makes it easier to rack up Loyalty Points. This card helps me reach my status goal by netting me up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per elite status qualification year (10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points).

Related: How I booked Japan Airlines first class for just 80K American Airlines AAdvantage miles

Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards is now the only major U.S. airline loyalty program that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles. That means you don't have to spend an outrageous amount of money to earn top-tier status (though you can choose to earn status via spending). Alaska Atmos Rewards members can now also earn points on award redemptions, which has driven my status earnings this year.

I've spent my Atmos Rewards points on award tickets flying Cathay Pacific within Asia and a flight from Seattle to Hong Kong in business class, a Hawaiian Airlines first-class flight from Honolulu to New York and an American Airlines flight from New York to Prague.

So far, I've earned the 40,000 status points required for Gold status this year through a combination of reward flights and spending on my . In addition to earning 1 status point for every $2 spent, with no spending cap, I also earn 10,000 status points each year on my account anniversary and 3 points per $1 on all foreign transactions with this card. This makes it worth the $395 annual fee, to me.

(Cardholders with the $95 annual fee earn 1 status point per $3 spent, also with no spending cap.)

While Alaska's partnership with American Airlines means I can fly Alaska flights with my top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status, I'm considering pursuing an even higher Alaska status in 2027. One of the main reasons is that Alaska upgrades its top-tier Titanium members (and a companion) to business class on international flights on the day of departure. Those with status are also now eligible for complimentary upgrades on Hawaiian Airlines flights. I've gotten upgraded on Hawaiian a few times with my status.

I'm also putting a ton of spending on my Summit card now, since Atmos Rewards has a partnership with Bilt that gets you 3 Atmos Rewards points for every dollar of rent you put on the card.

All that spending could help get me a good chunk of the way toward top-tier Titanium status, which requires 135,000 status points. I need to make a decision soon about my 2027 focus, but I haven't been able to cut the cord with American Airlines and fully commit to Alaska... at least not yet.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Alaska Atmos Rewards elite status

Over the past few years, my status with Delta has been on a steep decline. I enjoyed several years as a Delta Diamond, but it's just become too expensive (28,000 Medallion Qualification Dollars, to be exact) to earn top-tier status.

I only qualified for entry-level Silver last year, which requires 5,000 MQDs. A friend threw me a bone and gifted me second-tier Gold status, which typically requires 10,000 MQDs, but I'm not on track to re-earn it for 2027.

So far, my total spending this year is just 7,338 MQDs. This includes 5,000 MQDs just for holding the and the .

The $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) for the Delta Reserve is steep, but it's often worth it for those chasing status. It's just not enough of a boost to get me even to Gold status.

The Reserve card does give 1 MQD for every $10 you spend on the card. Technically, you could spend your way to status, but there's no way I can put that much spending on my Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card. While I still like the card for all its perks, I'm no longer putting much spending on it.

While I am likely to drop down to Silver for 2027, I'll still fly Delta occasionally.

I've made great use of SkyMiles over the years. Last year, I lucked out with an award from Mexico City International Airport (MEX) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and then to Brisbane Airport (BNE) in Delta One. There was a brief moment when the flight was available for just 73,000 SkyMiles one-way. I jumped at the opportunity to fly in Delta One on the more-than-14-hour flight to Australia.

Despite being what I'd consider the least valuable airline currency, SkyMiles remain appealing, and I'll keep my Reserve and Platinum cards for the long term. I've gotten a lot of use out of the statement credits that come with holding the cards.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

I added another airline elite status to my collection in 2026: Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, which I received simply for signing up for the (see rates and fees) and carrying the card. This would typically require earning 25,000 Status Qualifying Credits through the airline.

Unfortunately, I haven't had many opportunities to actually fly with Air Canada, and I've even let some of my valuable eUpgrade credits expire unused.

Still, I've become increasingly interested in the Air Canada Aeroplan program, especially because of its extensive network of airline partners and the ability to book some excellent business-class award flights through them.

One of my favorite redemptions using my welcome bonus on that card was booking a business-class flight on Emirates from Rio de Janeiro to Buenos Aires for just 56,000 Aeroplan points. It's a fascinating fifth-freedom route, and I was especially excited about the opportunity to finally experience Emirates.

I was also able to book Swiss Airlines business class from Cairo to Zurich and then on to New York for just 85,000 Aeroplan points.

Looking ahead, I'm particularly intrigued by Aeroplan's generous stopover rules. The program allows travelers to add a stopover of more than 24 hours on eligible international one-way award itineraries for just 5,000 additional points. That's an incredible opportunity to visit two destinations on a single award ticket.

Even though I haven't gotten much use out of my Air Canada elite status, Aeroplan remains one of the most interesting airline loyalty programs in my points-and-miles arsenal. I'm hoping to put more of those points — and perhaps some of those elite benefits — to work in the year ahead.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

Another new status for me is United Airlines MileagePlus Premier Silver. I actually did a status challenge with United late last year, and enjoyed a few months of top-tier United Premier 1K status, but I wasn't able to complete the challenge to unlock it for a full year.

Still, I've really enjoyed flying United more. It's easier to get to their hub at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) from my New York City apartment, and I ended up flying and earning enough this year to earn the entry-level United Silver status, which requires at least 6,000 Premier qualifying points or 15 Premier Qualifying Flights and 5,000 PQPs. (In 2027, United is ditching PQFs, making status eligible only through PQPs.)

Silver status allows me to get priority boarding, extra-legroom seats at check-in 24 hours before flying and standby for earlier flights.

During the brief window I had 1K status, I really enjoyed boarding ahead of Group 1.

Related: 5 last-minute ways to earn United elite status this year

More importantly, during my challenge I signed up for the (see rates and fees), which got me a good stash of United miles that I've used effectively.

I was able to spend just 85,000 United miles for a one-way business-class flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark this year, and I've just booked another business-class flight from Sydney, Australia, back to New York for 85,000 United miles.

I've earned a total of 8,640 PQPs toward status this year, but I'm unlikely to earn the more than 3,000 more I'd need for Premier Gold before the end of the year. I think Silver status is just fine for me for now.

I've loved having top-tier World of Hyatt Globalist status again this year. I've been able to use suite upgrades at several stand-out properties this year, including the Grand Hyatt Kauai Resort & Spa in Hawaii, the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro in Brazil and the Hyatt Regency Cairo West in Egypt.

Globalist benefits include guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, free breakfast and better upgrade odds.

This year, I've earned top-tier status organically with stays all over the world. I especially loved finally getting to check out the newly renovated Park Hyatt Tokyo and to stay at the Park Hyatts in Shanghai and Beijing.

While earning Globalist status requires 60 nights at Hyatt hotels per year, I've already stayed 79 nights this year. I may try to hit 90 nights in 2026, so I can earn another Milestone Rewards choice.

I also plan on keeping both my (see rates and fees) and my (see rates and fees) to help me get more elite nights toward status each year.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

I've also been putting Hyatt stays on my World of Hyatt Credit Card to earn 4 points per dollar spent at Hyatt hotels and resorts. You also earn two elite nights for every $5,000 you put on the personal card.

To me, World of Hyatt is the most valuable hotel loyalty program because I often get upgraded and never have to fight for late checkout. Hyatt points also stretch very far, especially compared with Hilton and Marriott. I already have trips on the books next year for Alila Villas Uluwatu in Indonesia, Park Hyatt Milan and Hyatt Paris Madeleine.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

Hilton Honors elite status is one of the easiest achievements to reach. Although I stayed at a Hilton hotel only a few times this year, I maintained Diamond status. How did I manage that? It's a perk of holding .

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Hilton Honors elite status

The card comes with Hilton Diamond status for as long as you hold it. Despite a $550 annual card fee (see rates and fees), the card is still worth keeping.

There are other valuable inclusions, such as up to $400 to spend at Hilton resorts every year (up to $200 in statement credits from January to June and another up to $200 in statement credits from July to December), up to $200 in statement credits for eligible flight purchases (up to $50 per quarter) and a free night when you open the account and reach your annual card anniversary.

Last year, I used my free night at the chic Conrad Tokyo on a room that would have been more than $1,100. This year, I used it at the Hilton Tokyo in a room that went for more than $650 a night.

I used one of my $200 stay statement credits last year at the Hilton Tangier Al Houara Resort & Spa in Morocco, and the other at Resorts World Las Vegas. In past years, I've also used it at Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort and Hilton Hawaiian Village Waikiki Beach Resort in Hawaii.

I also use the airline fee credits regularly. When using the Aspire card to pay, you get up to $50 in statement credits for eligible airline purchases each quarter.

Thanks to this card, I've had Hilton Diamond status since 2020.

Related: No suite upgrade but charm aplenty: What it's like staying at one of Hilton's SLH properties as a top-tier elite

While I have had some nice stays at Hilton properties — including the stunning Conrad Bora Bora Nui — over the years, I've rarely been upgraded despite my Diamond status. Still, the statement credits alone justify keeping the Aspire card and my Diamond status for 2027, even if I don't have as much luck getting upgrades with Hilton as I do with Hyatt.

I will earn Platinum Elite status with Marriott again this year just for holding a credit card.

In the past, I've been content with the Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status I receive courtesy of the ; it gives status in several hotel programs, including Marriott Bonvoy (enrollment required).

Related: Guide to Marriott and Hilton elite status with the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum

Then in 2022, American Express surprised everyone by announcing that holders of the would get Platinum Elite status for as long as they hold the card. I jumped at the chance to apply for it. As a result, I've held Platinum Elite status since then.

I've spent more than two dozen nights at Marriott properties this year and having Platinum Elite status certainly enhanced my trips with benefits like guaranteed late checkout, lounge access and complimentary breakfast. I even got an upgrade at the Ritz-Carlton in Hong Kong.

I used the annual free night that comes with the Brilliant card two years in a row at the lakefront Hotel President Wilson in Geneva, Switzerland. Last year, I used it for London's Bankside Hotel.

Related: 30 best Marriott hotels in the world that you can book with points

So far, I've booked 46 Marriott nights this year. I won't try to get the higher Titanium status — which requires 75 nights — though the idea of opening the is intriguing. Each year you hold the card, you receive 15 elite night credits toward the next level of Marriott Bonvoy elite status.

At least for now, though, I'll keep the personal Brilliant card open and enjoy Platinum Elite status without worrying about how many nights I need to stay.

Related: Last-minute strategies to earn Marriott Bonvoy elite status

Like my other hotel statuses, I have Platinum Elite status with IHG One Rewards by virtue of holding its hotel-branded card.

Last year, I stayed at several memorable IHG properties, including the Kimpton Fitzroy in London, the InterContinental Porto in Portugal, the Kimpton Overland Hotel in Atlanta and the InterContinental Ljubljana in Slovenia. This year, I've checked into the Hotel InterContinental Bordeaux Le Grand and WM Hotel in Sai Kung (a Vignette property) near Hong Kong.

Despite staying only seven nights at IHG hotels in 2026, I will maintain IHG Platinum Elite status simply by holding the IHG One Rewards Select Credit Card (no longer open to new applicants). In addition to elite status, my favorite perk of this card is its free night award worth up to 40,000 points, which I've used at the Kimpton Armory Hotel in Bozeman, Montana, and the aforementioned InterContinental in Portugal.

The information for the IHG One Rewards Select card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The new version of the card is the (see rates and fees), which also provides Platinum Elite status. It also comes with a fourth night free on award stays and the ability to add points to your 60,000-point anniversary free night certificate (these perks aren't available on the Select card). The annual fee is $350.

I'll keep my IHG card for status (and a free night) again next year. I'm also sitting on a nice stash of points, so odds are I'll enjoy some great redemptions in the not-too-distant future — though I don't have any IHG stays planned so far in 2027.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning IHG One Rewards elite status

The last status I'll mention is with Starbucks, since I'm a regular at the cafe near my apartment.

That regularity earned me top-tier Reserve status in the Starbucks Rewards program, which was overhauled earlier this year.

Reserve status earns 0.7 Stars more per dollar spent than entry-level Green status (for a total of 1.7 Stars per dollar) and requires earning an eye-watering 2,500 Stars over a rolling 12-month period to reach. That's 2,000 more Stars than necessary for the next-lowest tier, Gold.

It may not be the most rewarding program in the world — especially if you have a lower status tier — but the savings I get through the program add up and have me just as hooked on it as I am on my preferred hotel and airline programs.

Related: Why I got top-tier status with Starbucks and enjoy it — despite the reduced earnings for some

I've thought about going fully free agent and stopping my pursuit of status. But the truth is, I have fun on the hamster wheel, and the perks really make the game worth playing.

I'll have top-tier status with American, Hyatt and Hilton again next year. I'm excited to use more of my perks in 2027, and I will report back on my 2028 plans next year.

If you're considering going for status, you should really do the math to see if the extra costs are worth the benefits you get. It's harder to earn status these days, and the benefits keep getting whittled down. Don't do it unless you know you will use the perks and that you can do it without spending a small fortune.

It can be more cost-effective to get a credit card that automatically gives you some status perks, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

At least think about it. I'm not sure I'm the best at following my own advice.

#6257. American Airlines Dropped One Bogus Award Fee. Alaska Airlines And Air Canada Keep Collecting Theirs.

American Airlines once charged members $75 to book an award ticket close to departure. The airline eventually eliminated that fee, but a new account from its former loyalty chief offers a revealing reminder: the work used to justify a charge can disappear long before the charge does.

On the latest Airlines Confidential podcast, former AAdvantage chief and American Airlines Chief Information Officer Maya Leibman discussed an airline fee she had trouble defending, as flagged by View From The Wing.

American continued collecting its close-in award booking fee after the ticketing process became automated. Members without an applicable elite waiver paid $75 when booking within 21 days of departure. Leibman recalled that “we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days,” even though the transaction was “all done automatically.”

American eliminated the fee in January 2020. Like Gary, I appreciate hearing a former executive acknowledge the tension with collecting money for an expedited process that no longer required anyone to expedite it. I would rather hear that candid admission than a strained argument trying to justify it.

I can also understand why manually processing an award ticket once required time and resources and understand why an airline might have charged more to complete that work shortly before departure. But when a computer issues the ticket, what exactly is being expedited?

The airline still has expenses, of course. Maintaining a reservation system costs money. So does operating a loyalty program. But those expenses also exist when someone books a ticket three months before departure and do not explain why an otherwise identical automated transaction should suddenly cost another $75 inside a 21-day window.

The more straightforward explanation is that American could collect the money, so it did.

Airlines do not price everything according to the cost of providing it, and I do not expect them to. A last-minute seat may command a premium because demand supports it. But if that is the rationale, call it a premium for booking at the last minute. Calling it a processing expense just makes frequent flyers jaded. And whatever you call it, customers are understandably going to hate it because it does not correlate to any legitimate expense unless you count the sunk cost of the investment in the automation system.

American dropped its fee, but I see the same problem today with partner award booking fees at Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards and Air Canada Aeroplan.

I covered the Atmos fee increase earlier this year. Aeroplan also spells out its charge in its flight reward policy and makes it clear when booking online or on the Air Canada app.

These are airline-imposed charges, of course, not government taxes, though they are often lumped into the same section to suggest that you’re paying taxes, not fees. Here, you can do the searching, select the flights, enter your information, and complete an ordinary booking online, yet still pay extra for the privilege of redeeming your points on a partner.

I consider these bogus fees. They are revenue-generating measures, and I will not defend them as some necessary surcharge for the work involved in issuing my ticket. But by bogus that doesn’t mean that I fail to understand why they are levied.

Yes, programs pay partner airlines for award travel, bu that is part of offering partner awards in the first place. It should already inform the economics of selling points and setting redemption prices. Collecting another cash charge from the member is a commercial choice.

For my family of four, the Atmos fee alone adds $160 to a round-trip partner award unless a waiver applies (and I don’t have the credit card right now). That is real money, especially when we are already redeeming a substantial number of points.

There is one concession I will make: these fees are published and displayed during booking. We can account for them when deciding what the points and the program are worth.

If an award costs 50,000 points plus taxes and a partner booking fee, that cash payment belongs in my valuation. I should not calculate the value of the redemption as though the fee does not exist.

A program with an annoying booking fee can still offer a better overall deal than a program without one. I would happily pay $20 to save thousands of points on an otherwise comparable itinerary. But that makes the redemption worthwhile despite the fee. It does not make the fee itself worthwhile.

The same applies when earning or buying points. If I expect to redeem primarily on partners, those charges reduce what I am willing to pay for the currency. Transparency lets us make that calculation, so at least there is that.

American Airlines deserves credit for eventually eliminating its $75 close-in award booking fee. Leibman’s recollection helps explain why members were right to question it: the process became automated, but the charge remained.

Partner award booking fees at Atmos Rewards and Aeroplan strike me as similarly unappealing revenue measures. I still use both programs, and a good redemption can easily outweigh the extra cash required. But I bake those charges into my valuation rather than pretend they are justified by some special service I am receiving.

Sometimes a fee survives because collecting it is profitable, which his hardly breaking news, but something I appreciate Leibman confirming explicitly.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Hey… would sure be nice if we had better consumer protections, ya know, so that companies could stop getting away with screwing us… just an idea.

@1990 – this isn’t “screwing us” – it is a fee that a private business decides to impose. They could charge $500 to book an award ticket and the government shouldn’t do anything about it. It is up to the consumer to decide if the fee (like any other cost) is worth it to them. BTW, I agree the $20 partner booking fee is a rip off (and got the Summit card to avoid it) but it is ultimately up to a business to price their product as they see fit. The last thing we need is government price controls on business.

I wish the Atmos award change fee was $100 with a Summit waiver. Too many people (likely bots) were happy to camp inventory for months, then change their bookings close in. When award space is so limited, I’d rather it be more available to people who are actually going to fly. Higher fees and special treatment for flyers (likely elites) who carry the Summit for its other benefits would likely help with award availability. I know they’ll never jack it that high but a guy can dream

#6256. The Best Ski Resorts in Europe: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

For our 39th annual Readers’ Choice Awards, survey voters weighed in on their favorite ski resorts in Europe. Swiss resorts earned four of the top five spots, with Verbier claiming the number one ranking for the second consecutive year. Italy’s Olympic spotlight helped it land an unprecedented five resorts on the list. The tiny ski resort of Gudauri in Georgia’s Caucasus Mountains made its debut in the rankings—proof that readers are venturing further afield for fresh tracks. Here are the ski resorts that you loved most, for both their diversity of terrain, excellent après ski scenes, and exceptional hotels.

The Caucasus Mountains may not have the cachet of the Alps or the Rockies, but there are plenty of reasons to make the journey to ski in Georgia. The ski passes are a bargain. The slopes are uncrowded. And the food rivals anything you’ll have in France or Italy. Gudauri, the country’s premier ski resort has just over 50 miles of groomed trails, plus freeriding opportunities. There’s a mom-and-pop vibe, with stalls at the base of the mountain selling wool-knit socks, and churchkhela, candle-like strings of nuts encased in a wax-like, grape juice. Travel Bar and La Suite are the main après ski spots (be warned, the local brandy, chacha, is like rocket fuel). Plan an early on-slope lunch at Cafe Vitamin, where you can dig into traditional dishes like khachapuri, molten cheese (often topped with an egg) baked into a shallow bread bowl.

Where to stay: Ski-in/ski-out Gudauri Lodge has 171 rooms across five categories and a sprawling open-air hot tub. Ati Ambavi is a boutique hotel with room decor inspired by cultural icons like Georgian-American ballet master George Balanchine and Georgian artist Niko Pirosmani. The Rooms Kazbegi hotel is a 40-minute drive from the ski resort but its mountain views, delicious Georgian restaurant, and hip vibe are worth the commute.

Stats: There are 14 lifts for nearly 50 miles of runs. One-day lift ticket from $27.

Located on the Italian side of the Matterhorn massif, the high-altitude ski resort of Cervinia is linked with the Swiss resort of Zermatt. The combined terrain is vast, making it possible to log serious mileage without repeating a run all day. The majority of slopes are geared toward beginners and intermediates and the on-piste dining options are exceptional. Many skiers cross the border just to lunch on pasta all'Amatriciana and sip Bombardinos (an Italian riff on eggnog). Cervino The One is a new cableway project connecting Breuil-Cervinia with Plateau Rosa/Testa Grigia in just over 15 minutes. The modern two-section 3S gondola by Leitner includes a mid-station at Plan Maison.

Where to stay: Stylish apartments at Saint Hubertus Resort have modern kitchens, marble bathrooms, and stone living rooms with fireplaces. The team at five-star Hermitage Hotel & Spa can arrange adventures ranging from snowshoeing to heliskiing.

Stats: There are 19 lifts for 72 runs. One-day lift ticket from $52; on the Ikon pass.

Located on the sunnier, Italian side of Mont Blanc, Courmayeur attracts both dedicated skiers and unapologetic sybarites who prefer to sip Aperol spritzes on terraces by day and dine on gourmet meals at night. The Skyway Monte Bianco cable car whisks skiers across the Italian-French border where they can test their mettle on 11-plus miles of spectacular off-piste slopes, including the bucket-list glacial run of the Vallée Blanche in Chamonix. The resort’s modernized snowmaking system guarantees snow on over 8o percent of the slopes, every day of the season. After the pistes close, the Courmayeur Cable Car continues running until midnight so you can dine at mountain-top restaurants like LaChaumière. You can also experience the adventure of a snowmobile climb to reach fancy alpine huts like Rifugio Monte Bianco.

Where to stay: Auberge de la Maison is the epitome of alpine romance. Most rooms have panoramic views of Mont Blanc and the spa features unique alpine therapies such as a hay bio-sauna.

Stats: One-day lift ticket from $83; there are 18 lifts for 33 trails.

When an Egyptian billionaire opened five-star The Chedi Andermatt hotel (more on that later) in 2013, it turned a relatively unknown ski area tucked between Zermatt and St. Moritz into an international ski destination. The largest ski area in the heart of Switzerland has such varied and vast terrain you never have to repeat a run. Gemsstock is a steep, free-riding playground while neighboring Nätschen is laced with cruise-y runs. And if you want something more mellow, you can easily link to the family-friendly slopes of Sedrun. When your legs get tired from all the skiing, the Matterhorn Gotthard railway (also included in the ticket) will take you back to Andermatt. This season, Andermatt-Sedrun will open two new chairlifts, the Val Val-Calmut and Val Val-Cuolm, doubling capacity to 2,400 skiers per hour. The culinary scene is more impressive than ever now that Swiss star chef Andres Caminada has opened an outpost of his IGNIV restaurant concept in Andermatt’s Reuss district.

Where to stay: The extravagant Chedi Andermatt has 123 spacious rooms and suites all boasting fireplaces, Hästens mattresses, and large balconies. Set aside plenty of time to soak in the spa’s hydrotherapy zone and indulge in the 16-foot-high, glass-walled, climate-controlled Cheese Tower or The Japanese, the hotel’s Michelin-star Japanese restaurant.|

Stats: Average price for a one-day lift ticket is $120; the Andermatt-Sedrun-Disentis ski region comprises 33 lifts for 93 marked pistes; on the Epic Pass.

Located on the ridge between Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, Abetone is Central Italy’s largest ski region. Many call it Florence’s secret ski resort as it’s just a 90-minute drive from the city. The family-friendly resort is made up of four interconnected valleys. Local ski champ Zeno Colò designed a handful of runs including the “Zeno” slopes in the Valley of Luce. There’s also a dedicated Nordic skiing area. The slopes are rarely crowded, especially in the afternoons, which are dedicated to long leisurely lunches at rifugios like La Selletta and Monte Gomito.

Where to stay: Val di Luce Spa Resort has spacious family suites that sleep four to six, many with well-equipped kitchens. The spa is a highlight with a pool housed in a Louvre-like glass pyramid so you can gaze at the starry night sky.

Stats: There are 17 lifts for just over 30 miles of runs. One-day lift ticket from $60.

Perched at 5,950 feet, this remote ski town in Lombardy is nicknamed “Little Tibet.” Its four, high-altitude snowparks served as the Winter Olympic stage for freestyle skiing and snowboarding. And its party scene is just as rowdy as its terrain. Set at the base of the Carosello 3000 cable car beneath a huge circus tent, Stalet is an après ski institution known for its crazy costumes, tabletop dancing, and DJ sets. On the Mottolino slopes, Camanel di Planon is an old-school mountain hut with a panoramic terrace and daily 1p.m. music-and-dance show. The best way to arrive at Milky’s Disco Club is via a copper slide at the entrance (stairs are also an option). Party nights are often themed and costumes are highly recommended.

Where to stay: Hotel Spöl is a five-star, adults-only property in Valtellina with a new longevity-focused spa that offers therapies like cryo and molecular hydrogen boosters.

Stats: There are 32 lifts for 78 runs. One-day lift ticket from $74.

Zermatt, surrounded by the Alps’ tallest peaks, has 223 miles of runs in four huge ski areas—some at an altitude of over 10,000 feet, so snow here lingers well beyond the winter season. This enchanting, alpine village lies at the foot of the Matterhorn, Switzerland's most famous mountain, and has plenty of modern touches, like its swanky après-ski diversions and state-of-the-art lift system, recently enhanced this season with the new 6-seater Patrullarve chairlift. Horse-drawn sleighs are the preferred choice of transportation in the car-free village. On the slopes, be sure to stop for the burger at Chez Vrony (reservations a must) and a glass of bubbles at the tiny Champagne bar at the end of the Sunnega run. The new Matterhorn Glacier Ride II now links the entire stretch between Zermatt and Cervinia by cable car, connecting the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise mountain station with the Testa Grigia valley station. Cervino The One is an ambitious new cableway project on the Italian side, connecting Breuil-Cervinia with Plateau Rosa/Testa Grigia in just over 15 minutes.

Where to stay: Grand dame Mont Cervin Palace and modern-luxe Schweizerhof Zermatt, both offer prime central locations and every imaginable amenity. Just above the village, slope-side CERVO Mountain Resort has an ashram-inspired spa with an expansive network of outdoor pools, saunas, and soaking tubs.Riffelalp Resort is another favorite located directly on the slopes, and the Omnia is beautifully nestled into the mountains just above the village.

Stats: There are 55 lifts for 147 runs. One-day lift ticket from $87; on the Ikon Pass.

Poised on a south-facing mountain plateau, Alpe d'Huez is aptly nicknamed “Island in the Sun,” averaging 300 days of sunshine per year. This vast ski area connects several charming villages—Huez, Vaujany, Oz-en-Oisans, Auris-en-Oisans, and Villard-Reculas—and contains terrain to satisfy every skier, from cruisey blues to 10-mile-long La Sarenne, the lengthiest black diamond run in France. Its high elevation—Pic Blanc summit reaches 10,925 feet—also makes it reliably snow sure. On-mountain restaurants, like L'Alpette Chez Passoud, served made-from-scratch regional dishes like tartiflette. And there’s a lively après ski scene anchored by iconic party spot La Folie Douce. Each March, electronic music festival Tomorrowland, takes over the slopes.

Where to stay: Club Med’s all-inclusive ski packages offer great value and the brand’s Alpe d'Huez location is perched at 6,100 feet, delivering ski-in/ski-out access and sensational views. The 5-star Daria-1 Nor hotel, part of the French Les Étincelles Collection, offers direct access to the Alpe Express gondola, and its spa is the ultimate sanctuary for recovery with a hammam, contrast therapy, and a Himalayan salt wall. Hotel Pic Blanc has cozy chalet vibes and a fantastic restaurant.

Stats: There are 84 lifts for 111 runs. One-day lift ticket from $65.

With three nearby airports—Munich, Salzburg, and Innsbruck—Kitzbühel is easily Austria’s most popular holiday resort. The legendary alpine sports town has it all: posh hotels, a picturesque 750-year-old town center, a lively après-ski scene along quaint, cobblestone streets, and unsurpassed skiing that includes 11 renowned ski schools and the most demanding course on the World Cup circuit. With more than 60 mountain huts and restaurants, there are plenty of delicious options to refuel, or lounge leisurely over lunch on the slopes. The resort also has a stellar line-up of winter events, including the Sound Escape music festival (December 11 -12, 2026) and the Bendura Bank Snow Polo World Cup (Jan. 15-17, 2027).

Where to stay: Hotel Schloss Lebenberg, a medieval hillside castle overlooking the village that earns high marks for its stellar service, dining room, and ornate, Gothic-style décor. For affordability and convenience, check out the Henri boutique hotel by the train station.

Stats: 58 lifts for 96 runs covering 145 miles. One-day lift tickets average $92; on the Ikon Pass.

Megève may not have the haute party scene of, say, St. Moritz, or the breadth of sporty-centric Courchevel, but it still has plenty to tout. Two ski areas are covered with nearly 250 miles of runs linked by state-of-the-art cable cars. Skiers can choose from 50-plus on-mountain restaurants, like the excellent La Ferme de Mon Père. A charming, car-free city center featuring an open-air ice rink, cobbled streets, horse-drawn sleighs, as well as a number of smart boutiques makes Megève a family favorite.

Where to stay: The resort's primary patrons—streams of well-heeled Parisians looking to escape the city—reserve rooms at Relais & Châteaux Flocons de Sel, or the Les Fermes de Marie, a tiny mountain chalet where the rooms have fur throws, wood-beamed ceilings, and stone accent walls. Four Seasons Hotel Megève and 12-room Le Chalet, from Zannier Hotels, both offer five-star service.

Stats: There are 112 lifts for nearly 250 runs for the Évasion Mont-Blanc ski area. One-day lift tickets from $60. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited Pass starts at $116 and includes 10 ski areas and nearly 450 miles of slopes across three countries; on the Mountain Collective Pass.

Val Thorens is a resort of superlatives. Europe’s highest ski resort offers one of the continent’s longest ski seasons, running from November 21, 2026, to May 2, 2027, and is part of Les 3 Vallées, the world’s largest linked ski area, with more than 370 miles of runs. This winter, the resort is expanding its appeal with new dining spots, thrilling off-slope activities and a fresh high-altitude experience. At Caron 3200, perched at 10,498 feet, visitors can embark on a virtual-reality ascent of Everest, immersing themselves in the journey to the world’s highest summit without leaving the Alps. For those seeking a different kind of adrenaline rush, the resort is introducing Mountain Kart Xperience, while the Cosmojet toboggan run offers three miles of exhilarating downhill fun. The Bee zipline adds another dose of adventure, soaring 5,905 feet above the slopes. The dining scene is also evolving: Le Bouchon Alpin brings a taste of Lyonnais and Savoyard classics, Le Neva serves contemporary French cuisine inspired by seasonal ingredients, and Zig Zag Café opens as the resort’s first dedicated coffee shop. Meanwhile, the international freeride spotlight returns to Val Thorens from January 25 to 30, 2027, when the Freeride World Tour brings the world’s best skiers and snowboarders to its dramatic high-mountain terrain. The après ski scene has long been legendary, known for party institutions like La Folie Douce and low-key gathering spots such as La Timbale, a tapas bar in the heart of the village.

Where to stay: Five-star Hótel Pashmina for the outdoor spa with stunning mountain views.

Stats: 25 lifts for 93 miles of pistes. One-day lift ticket for Val Thorens starting at $77. One-day lift ticket for the Three Valleys $98; on the Epic Pass.

The oldest winter holiday resort in the world is as elegant and exclusive as it gets. As if St. Moritz wasn't already blessed enough at nearly 6,000 feet above sea level, the sun shines 322 days a year, pairing with the dry air for what’s known as a “Champagne climate.” But it’s the world-class hotels and restaurants, chic shopping, and excellent skiing on- and off-piste that draw celebrities and royalty alike. The iconic alpine city is equally famous for its unique events on the frozen lake St. Moritz: the Snow Polo World Cup St. Moritz, the White Turf horse racing and the ICE car show. The restaurant scene has never been more varied, from cult Italian franchise Crazy Pizza and Greek hotspot Neora at the Grand Hotel des Bains Kempinski St. Moritz to Beefbar at Grace La Margna.

Where to stay: A room in the Serlas Wing at alpine grand dame Badrutt's Palace Hotel, which has been indulging A-listers since 1896, or at the Kulm Hotel—one of our Gold List favorites—can do no wrong.

Stats: There are 58 lifts for 88 runs. One-day lift tickets range from $45 to $100; on the Ikon Pass.

Lech Zürs may lack the bling of areas like St. Moritz and Cortina d’Ampezzo, but that’s part of its charm. Behind traditional farmhouse facades you’ll find chic, family-run boutiques, art galleries, and stylish hotels and chalets. The village of 1,600 may be tiny, but it boasts one of the highest density of award-winning restaurants in the world (Rote Wand Chef’s Table at Rote Wand Gourmet Hotel is a must). And of course there’s the draw of its excellent snowfall and the famed White Ring, a circuit of nearly 14 miles that links Lech, Zürs, Zug, and Oberlech. Two modern cable cars make the slopes even more accessible.

Where to stay: Five-star Hotel Almhof Schneider is the epitome of alpine elegance, with a serious art collection, serene spa, and a 25,000-bottle wine cellar. The family behind the property also recently opened two, design-centric chalets, Haus W and Chalet Sonnenhof. Boutique stay Hotel Kristiania was originally established by Olympic skier Othmar Schneider, and his family continues the hotel’s legacy of hospitality. The Yurt, a salon-inspired après bar within a Kyrgyz-style tent, takes up residency on the hotel grounds this season.

Stats: Part of the Arlberg, Austria’s largest inter-linked ski area, 85 lifts and cable cars can access more than 180 miles of marked slopes and 120-plus miles of backcountry runs. One-day lift ticket from $95; on the Epic Pass.

Chamonix-Mont Blanc’s expansive backcountry and gnarly terrain make it a bucket-list destination for serious skiers. Host to the first winter Olympics in 1924, the pedestrian-friendly town oozes alpine charm and, despite the mountain’s extreme reputation, there are plenty of beginner and intermediate runs. Riding the Aiguille du Midi, the highest cable car in Western Europe is a must simply for the views. From the top, experienced skiers can schuss down the legendary Vallée Blanche, 12.4-mile glacier descent in the heart of Mont-Blanc Massif. A guide is essential for the descent and Chamonix has the world’s oldest and largest guiding organization. The eclectic dining scene draws on flavors from around the world. Essential reservations include Mumma, which specializes in Asian and South American fusion cuisine, and Yumidori, a Japanese spot helmed by a sushi world champ. Restaurant Le 3842, one of the highest restaurants in Europe, serves a three-course lunch atop the Aiguille du Midi.

Where to stay: La Folie Douce Hotel has a hip vibe, a lively après scene and an unbeatable location in the heart of Chamonix, with a ski lift steps from the front door. For over-the-top luxury, book a stay at Hameau Albert 1er. The five-star hotel has 33 rooms, two suites and two stand-alone chalets and a Michelin-star restaurant. Le Collectionist’s portfolio of luxury chalets range from three to 12 bedrooms.

Stats: There are 82 lifts for 91 runs. One-day lift ticket from $55; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective Pass. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited Pass starts at $85 and includes 10 ski areas and nearly 450 miles of slopes across three countries.
